545.content: Euergetia was one of Remuria's four Harmosts, called the benefactrix. The weapon story of Symphonist of Scents shows her using her power to let conquered, homesick people taste their native dishes in their imaginations. She perished in Remuria's destruction.

546.content:
Tale of "Durin" (also: Tale of Durin, Durin's storybook, the book of Durin, Andersdotter's magic book): Tale of "Durin" is a quest item from the Draco Rubedo Chapter (6.2), Durin's Story Quest. It is a replica, made by the Hexenzirkel witch Alice, of the unfinished storybook left by Andersdotter ("M"), Durin's creator and mother. The original had to end up with Durin so he could write his own ending. The replica has no magical properties but keeps every twist of the story.

Alice gave the replica to the Traveler at the end of The Solution of Fate, saying that a witness to the tale deserves a keepsake. The player can use it to re-read all the storybook panels from The Magic Known as Storytelling; panels reflect the choices made during the quest.

Lore: The original book was a joint work of the Hexenzirkel's witches, but Andersdotter died before finishing her part and left a great regret. She made sure Alice would give the book to Durin, whom she thought the only one who could resolve it. In the Story Quest the Traveler and Paimon help him fill the book's clues, entering the story world several times. The finale shows a simulated Simulanka-like world where Durin must break out of the story, and he receives his mother's pen and continues the tale. In post-quest dialogue Venti remarks that a line about Durin and Dvalin flying together over Mondstadt now describes a happy ending.

Appearance: The in-game icon is a storybook; no further description is given in item text. The original was a magic book, and the quest depicts the story world with a Dodoco narrator.

Owners: Original: made by Hexenzirkel witches including Andersdotter, entrusted to Durin through Alice. Replica: Alice made it and gave it to the Traveler.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 it remains a quest item in the Traveler's possession. The story of the original book is complete; Durin continues writing his own story.

547.comment: Tale of "Durin": The Solution of Fate
547.content: In The Solution of Fate, the finale of Durin's Story Quest, the book pulls the group into a story world in which Durin must defy the fate of the original dragon. His mother appears as a manifestation, hands him her pen so he can keep writing, and he wins his own ending. Alice then gives the Traveler a replica of the book.

548.content:
Tales Carried by the Northwind (also: Tales Carried by the Northwind (book)): It reads as a memorial anthology. Its fragments are elegies and heroic verse about leaders who held the title of Starshyna, and about the cost of leadership to those who followed them.

Appearance: A 3-star one-volume book collection, found on a box near Kofitse in Piramida.

Lore: Sergei Semyonovich Mayakov: one poem. An old man with a weapon stands against towering black waves while a voice in the mist reproaches him for the deaths of young men who trusted him, the orphans he adopted, the unsent distress signal and the fallen Lighthouse. He turns to the ocean and polishes his axe once more.

Owners: No owner; it is a loose book in Piramida.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 3-star Book Collection added in 6.3, found near Kofitse in Piramida.

549.comment: Tales Carried by the Northwind: Starshyna Verse
549.content: The book collects verse about Starshynas, attributed to Silvestr Petrovich Solovei and Sergei Semyonovich Mayakov. It is damaged and fragmentary, so any claim about the people or events behind the poems should be framed as what the verse says rather than as established history.

550.content:
Tamayuratei no Ohanashi (also: Tamayuratei, the lantern youkai's polearm): Tamayuratei no Ohanashi is a four-star polearm of the Youkai series, obtained during the Version 5.4 event Enchanted Tales of the Mikawa Festival. Its text tells of an invisible youkai who took the form of a spectral flame, stole stories at hearths and braziers and retold them at banquets of wandering spirits, and was named "Tamayuratei" by the kitsune chief Hakushin. After the Cataclysm it became a messenger of battle reports and wore itself away.

Appearance: The weapon is a lantern-topped polearm. The wiki notes that its lantern has dynamic night-time lighting when effects are set high (a client detail, not lore); the item text does not describe its look.

Lore: The text begins with spectral flames drifting through the wilds and an invisible, secret-loving youkai taking the form of such a flame, flitting from hearth to brazier to steal stories from people chatting over tea. It retold them at banquets of wandering spirits, for amusing the great while they drank was the purpose of the Otogishu. At one such evening Hakushin, chief of the kitsune, sighed that she wished time could stop, and raised her sake cup to give the lowly youkai on stage the title "Tamayuratei".

Owners: No human owner is named; the story is about an unnamed youkai who bears the title "Tamayuratei".

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star polearm of the Youkai series. Base ATK 44, secondary stat Energy Recharge 6.7%. Passive "Busybody's Running Light" raises ATK and Movement SPD by 10% for 10s after using an Elemental Skill. Obtained in the 5.4 event "Enchanted Tales of the Mikawa Festival".

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a storyteller's lantern: good for scenes about gossip, festival evenings and forgotten loyalty.

551.content:
Tenacity of the Millelith (also: Flower of Accolades, Ceremonial War-Plume, Orichalceous Time-Dial, Noble's Pledging Vessel, General's Ancient Helm): Tenacity of the Millelith is a 4- and 5-star artifact set for Liyue's soldiers. Its five pieces are a golden flower, a falcon-feather plume, a sun-and-moon time-dial, a golden oath cup and a general's helmet, and their item text commemorates the Millelith who held the Chasm against the Abyss alongside a nameless yaksha, dying there so civilians could escape.

Added in version 1.5. The text is Liyue folk memory about an event 500 years before the present, in the time of the Cataclysm. Rex Lapis is said to have sent the Millelith to defend the Chasm mines when the Abyss flooded in; the soldiers who stayed to cover the retreat are remembered in the Millelith's ceremonial dress.

Appearance: Ceremonial military gear of Liyue: a flower made of gold leaf, a plume from a high-altitude bird of prey worn on parade, a bronze time-dial powered by sunlight and moonlight, a golden cup used to swear oaths, and a splendid ancient helmet which looks new again once the dust is cleaned away.

Lore: Rex Lapis is said to have ordered the Millelith to defend the Chasm mines when the Abyss flooded in. Fighting beside a nameless yaksha, a rearguard stayed behind to cover the civilians' escape and fell there; Millelith ceremonial dress (golden flower, feather plume) honours them.

Owners: No owner is named. The text speaks of Millelith soldiers, their commander and a nameless yaksha; the wiki links the yaksha to Bosacius.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): obtained from the Ridge Watch domain and the Artifact Strongbox. 2-piece: HP +20%. 4-piece: when an Elemental Skill hits an opponent, all nearby party members gain ATK +20% and Shield Strength +30% for 3s, triggerable once per 0.5s, including while the wearer is off-field.

552.comment: Tenacity of the Millelith: Tenacity of the Millelith
552.content: Artifact set whose item text honours the Millelith soldiers and a nameless yaksha who died defending the Chasm mines from the Abyss at the time of the Cataclysm, about 500 years ago.

553.comment: Tenacity of the Millelith: The Chasm stand (item-text account)
553.content: In the folk account of the Tenacity of the Millelith set, a meteorite crater in the Chasm turned the ground to Glazed Sand Crystal. When the Abyss flooded in, Rex Lapis sent the Millelith to defend the mines; the troops escorted civilians out, and a rearguard stayed with a nameless yaksha and fell in the Chasm. The Abyss receded, the glaze sands shone again, and the yaksha vanished. Treat the details as legend: the text is partly contradictory about whether the yaksha acted on Rex Lapis's orders.

554.comment: Tenacity of the Millelith: Millelith ceremonial plume and golden flower
554.content: The set explains Millelith ceremonial dress: the golden flower honours the dead of the Chasm, and the feather plume worn on ceremonial occasions is said to have been inspired by the yaksha's torn plumage. The plumes raise civilian morale and awe foreign visitors.

555.content:
Teyvat Travel Guide (also: Teyvat Geographic Special Edition, Alice's Mondstadt Diaries, Alice's Travels in Liyue, Alice's Inazuma Diaries): The Teyvat Travel Guide is a three-volume magazine series from the Adventurers' Guild. Under the heading 'Teyvat Geographic Special Edition', each issue is a short travel diary by Alice, covering Mondstadt, Liyue and Inazuma. Alice is a cheerful experimenter and the diaries treat sightseeing as an excuse for explosives, potions and mischief.

The descriptions say each issue introduces great sceneries across Teyvat. Vol. 3 first became available in the limited-time Hues of the Violet Garden event (2.6), and Kuroda continues to sell it afterwards.

Appearance: Glossy magazine issues whose cover reads 'Travel Guide' in the Teyvat script. Entries are headed by place names and written in the first person in a breezy, boastful, sometimes self-deprecating voice.

Lore: Vol. 1 (Mondstadt) visits Dadaupa Gorge, Starsnatch Cliff, Windrise, Falcon Coast, the Whispering Woods, Brightcrown Canyon and Stormterror's Lair. Vol. 2 (Liyue) visits Dihua Marsh and Wangshu Inn, Guili Plains, Jueyun Karst, Yaoguang Shoal and Guyun Stone Forest. Vol. 3 (Inazuma) visits Mt. Yougou and the Grand Narukami Shrine, Inazuma City, Tatarasuna and Yashiori Island.

Owners: No individual owner. Alice is the diarist; Lisa gives Vol. 1, Chang the Ninth gives Vol. 2, and Kuroda (and, for a time, Murata) sells Vol. 3.

Gameplay: Game note: a three-volume collectible book collection. Vol. 1 comes from Lisa's quest Lost Book, Vol. 2 from Chang the Ninth's quest Justice Is Its Own Reward, and Vol. 3 from the limited-time Hues of the Violet Garden event (2.6) and Kuroda's shop afterwards. No stats.

556.comment: Teyvat Travel Guide: Alice's Mondstadt Diaries
556.content: Vol. 1 records Alice's visits to Dadaupa Gorge, Starsnatch Cliff, Windrise, Falcon Coast, the Whispering Woods, Brightcrown Canyon and Stormterror's Lair, with several explosive proposals that Kaeya, Jean's Outrider and Lisa tactfully decline.

557.comment: Teyvat Travel Guide: Alice's Travels in Liyue
557.content: Vol. 2 records Alice at Dihua Marsh, Wangshu Inn, the Guili Plains, Jueyun Karst, Yaoguang Shoal and Guyun Stone Forest, with her companion Zhongli, a potion that left a checkpoint guard imitating everyone, and a boat prototype that exploded.

558.comment: Teyvat Travel Guide: Alice's Inazuma Diaries
558.content: Vol. 3 was first obtained during the Hues of the Violet Garden event in 2.6 and is later sold by Kuroda. It records Mt. Yougou, Inazuma City, Tatarasuna and Yashiori Island, including Alice's meetings with Yae Miko, Naganohara Ryuunosuke, Yoimiya, Kagami Gozen and Washizu.

559.content:
The Alley Flash (also: Alley Flash): The Alley Flash is a four-star sword of the Alley series: a straight, night-black longsword once carried by a thief who roamed Mondstadt's benighted streets. The item text tells of a young noble who stole it from his family's vault and used it, never staining it with blood, to rob the rich for the poor.

Appearance: Item text calls it a mighty, noble longsword as black as night, its darkened blade blending into nights when people feared lighting fires. It is said many later knightly swords, such as the Favonius Sword, were modelled on this design. A bard's song says it was blackened during the age of the aristocracy.

Lore: The young noble (identified by the wiki as Parsifal) read the tales and songs of his upright ancestors, which sowed rebellion in him. He left his venerable house, stole the sword, and hid in the streets, living among common folk in alleys and taverns and using his noble swordsmanship to rob the rich for the poor. The edge was never marred by blood, nor was the thief's heart.

Owners: Item text refers to a young noble turned thief; the wiki identifies him as Parsifal. He took it from his house's vault and buried it before leaving.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Alley-series four-star sword, base ATK 45, Elemental Mastery 12 secondary, passive 'Itinerant Hero'. Released in Version 1.4 via Weapon Event Wishes.

560.content:
The Bell (also: Bell greatsword, clock greatsword): The Bell is a four-star claymore of the Wanderer's Troupe series. It is a heavy greatsword with a clock set into it, whose internal mechanisms are long damaged. Its story belongs to Kreuzlied, a former Lawrence clan noble turned traitor who travelled with the Troupe.

Appearance: Item text describes a strange greatsword decorated with an exquisite clock. After the Troupe disbanded it was soaked in acid, which rusted the gears; it is still a lethal weapon. Its clockwork once gave the wielder and friends a combat rhythm.

Lore: Kreuzlied once belonged to the ruling Lawrence clan but became a traitor and outcast and travelled with the Wanderer's Troupe. In that era scholars and bards ignored history because the aristocracy preferred wilful ignorance of their own decay to history's judgement, yet they trembled at the sound of this blade, the toll of the bell of judgment.

Owners: Kreuzlied, who travelled with the Troupe.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Wanderer's Troupe-series four-star claymore, base ATK 42, HP 9% secondary, passive 'Rebellious Guardian' (a shield; damage rises while any shield protects the wearer). Available in the standard Wanderlust Invocation and event wishes.

561.content:
The Black Sword (also: Black Sword): The Black Sword is a 4-star sword from the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn, in the game since Version 1.0. The in-game short description calls it a pitch-black longsword that thirsts for violence and conflict. The full text is the parable of a bright white knight whose pursuit of justice slid into slaughter.

Its text ties to the Bloodstained Chivalry artifact set, and the wiki notes that the decoration atop the blade resembles that set's circlet.

Appearance: A pitch-black longsword with a decoration on top of the blade. The wiki notes the decoration strongly resembles the circlet of the Bloodstained Chivalry artifact set. In the story the knight's sword once hung at his hip with a mirror sheen before the bloodshed blackened it.

Lore: A blade that thirsts after fresh blood is awakened by its scent, and those who wield and nourish it keep killing until even a pure soul is blackened. The text tells of a white knight who rode to cut down injustice, beasts and fires, taught by the Wolf Pup in chivalry, justice and swordsmanship.

The knight recalls losing himself in cutting, slashing and piercing, feeling a tingle at the blade's meeting flesh and believing this was justice getting its due. A voice calls him a fool and says slaughter in the name of justice is still slaughter; he answers that it is justice.

Owners: The item text names no owner. The wiki links the white knight to Roland; see his entry for the details.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star sword, base ATK 42, CRIT Rate secondary stat. Passive Justice: Normal and Charged Attack DMG rises 20 to 40 per cent by refinement, and a CRIT hit from those attacks restores 60 to 100 per cent of ATK as HP, at most once every 5s. The healing can trigger even if the hit deals no damage to an invulnerable or shielded enemy. Obtained through the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn bundle.

562.comment: The Black Sword: The White Knight
562.content: The white knight of The Black Sword's text rode to cut down injustice and was taught by the Wolf Pup, but his zeal for justice turned into killing, blackening his sword and face until he wore an iron mask. The wiki links him to Roland. See Roland's and the Bloodstained Chivalry entries.

563.content:
The Byakuyakoku Collection (also: Byakuyakoku Collection, Collection of Byakuyakoku): The Byakuyakoku Collection is a five-volume set of old texts from Enkanomiya's Byakuyakoku era, obtained by completing the quest Collection of Dragons and Snakes. It holds a folk tale of the Profane Serpent, a creation chronicle, a hydrology study, vishap experiment records and a children's puzzle book.

Together the volumes show how the people of Enkanomiya understood their world before and after the arrival of Watatsumi Omikami.

Appearance: Item art shows a slate-like tablet book. The volumes take different in-world forms: a novel, a restricted chronicle, a land survey, laboratory records and a riddle book.

Lore: - Vol. 1, "The Serpent and Drakes of Tokoyokoku": a novel based on Watatsumi folktales. The sage Aberaku brings a sun to Enkanomiya and is imprisoned by the first Sunchild; years later a child finds a vast serpent who becomes the people's god.
- Vol. 2, "Before Sun and Moon": a restricted chronicle of the world's making and the people's fall into the dark.
- Vol. 3: a geography and hydrology of Byakuyakoku.
- Vol. 4: Bathysmal Vishap experiment records.
- Vol. 5: a children's riddle book.

Vol. 1 is a Watatsumi novel carried to Narukami Island by a merchant while its serpent god lived.

Owners: Not a unique item; a collectible set found in Enkanomiya after completing the quest.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-volume collectible book collection added in Version 2.4 with Enkanomiya; the whole set is obtained via the quest Collection of Dragons and Snakes.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's suggestion): treat each volume as a document with its own bias, written before the people returned to the surface. The creation chronicle is a Byakuyakoku account, and the book's riddles and parables are teaching tools, not proof. Do not use it to explain things the texts leave elided, and keep Enkanomiya revelations out of the mouths of characters who never read them.

564.comment: The Byakuyakoku Collection: Before Sun and Moon
564.content: "Before Sun and Moon" is the Byakuyakoku chronicle in Vol. 2 of the Collection, recording the world from its making by the Primordial One to the fall of the ancestors into the dark and the building of Helios. It names the Ruler of Time "Kairos", whose secret name is Istaroth, written in reverse, and calls the sage Abrax the builder of the sun. Ordinary people were forbidden to read it. It ends mid-record with armour approaching.

565.comment: The Byakuyakoku Collection: Bathysmal Vishap Experimental Records
565.content: Vol. 4 holds laboratory records of experiments on the Dragonheirs of the Depths under Watatsumi Omikami's direction. The researchers study heritable traits and intelligence in captive vishaps, then graft Omikami's blood into them after earlier failures. Their asides note that none of them died, and that the prophesied Dragon of Water must not be born in Enkanomiya.

566.content:
"The Catch" (also: The Catch, Ako Domeki's harpoon, Zaemon's barbed spear): "The Catch" is a four-star polearm: the favoured barbed spear of a famous Inazuman bandit, Ako Domeki. It began as a harpoon for catching fish and proved handy in battle; item text says he even pierced the enchanted, sword-armed puppet with it before carrying it off. It is bought with fish from the Inazuma Fishing Association.

Appearance: Item text calls it a barbed spear that was originally a fishing harpoon. No more detail is given.

Lore: The text is a monologue by Ako Domeki, called Zaemon. He says he was once master of the ship Seiraimaru, commanded over ten ships and was called the Deathless Oni of Seirai, but is now "a leaf floating upon the waves". Without Janome and the people marooned on the islands he doubts he would have made it home, and he finds Seirai changed, with no place left for him in the Inazuman Islands; even the "naggy, fretful old shrine maiden" is gone.

Owners: Ako Domeki, the bandit (historical.ako-domeki). No later owner is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star polearm. Base ATK 42, secondary stat Energy Recharge 10%. Passive "Shanty" raises Elemental Burst DMG and Elemental Burst CRIT Rate. Bought with fish from Kujirai Momiji of the Inazuma Fishing Association.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a keepsake of a boisterous, fond farewell; characters from Seirai may remember Ako Domeki warmly, while the Shogunate's side would remember him as a bandit.

567.content: Ako Domeki, called Zaemon, was a famous Inazuman bandit and former master of the ship Seiraimaru, nicknamed the Deathless Oni of Seirai. His farewell monologue in the weapon's text has him say that Seirai has changed and leave to see the edge of the world. His own entry in the archive carries his biography.

568.content:
The Daybreak Chronicles (also: Daybreak Chronicles, Dawning Song of Daybreak): The Daybreak Chronicles is a five-star bow released in version 6.2 (2025-12-03), part of the Hexerei series. Its description calls it a bow whose strings gather the "songs of resistance" carried on the wind, strong enough to tear boundless darkness apart with the light of daybreak. Its item story is the legend of Kreuzlied, a name that Mondstadt turned from a byword for failed rebels into a rallying cry.

Appearance: The in-game text gives no visual description beyond the image of a bow strung with songs: the resistance songs settle "as gentle tones upon these strings". Artwork details are not described in canon text.

Lore: The story opens with two comrades: a voice in the wind sings farewell, and the answer is that nobody will weep, since the night breeze will carry the tears away. It then tells of a traveling musical troupe that, as the tale goes, plotted to assassinate the ruling house; one member was a renegade noble called Kreuzlied, and a tune was written for him after the plot failed.

Kreuzlied was not his real name, which is lost. The word meant "The Quartering Song", after a cruel public punishment the aristocracy enjoyed watching. It became a byword for those who rose up and failed, and so a rallying cry for rebellion.

Owners: No owner is named in canon text. The bow belongs to the legend of Kreuzlied rather than to a particular wielder.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star bow, Base ATK 48, CRIT DMG secondary stat. Passive "Dawning Song of Daybreak": out of combat the wielder gains a large Normal Attack, Skill and Burst DMG bonus (60-120%) that decays in combat and is rebuilt by hits, even off-field; Hexerei: Secret Rite in the party makes hits rebuild it faster.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the bow suits scenes about folk songs, tavern ballads and the memory of failed uprisings in Mondstadt. Ordinary Mondstadters may know a verse of the song; the idea that many figures were each called Kreuzlied is specialist lore.

569.content: In the Daybreak Chronicles, Kreuzlied is the name of a renegade noble in a traveling musical troupe that plotted against the ruling house and failed. The word means "The Quartering Song" in the old tongue, after a brutal execution, and became a byword for failed rebels and a rebel rallying cry. The man's real name is lost.

570.content:
The Exile (also: Exile's Flower, Exile's Feather, Exile's Pocket Watch, Exile's Goblet, Exile's Circlet): The Exile is an Energy Recharge artifact set (3 and 4 star, added 1.0), called Legacy in the Adventurer Handbook. Its five pieces mourn an aristocrat's carefree childhood, a family feud that wrecked his house, and a lonely exile in which he kept only a few treasured objects. The wiki links him to Parsifal and the Eberhart feud; the texts name no one.

The pieces are Exile's Flower, Exile's Feather, Exile's Pocket Watch, Exile's Goblet and Exile's Circlet.

Appearance: Heirloom and travel keepsakes: a faded flower, a sapphire-blue feather, a delicate childhood pocket watch, a broken silver family goblet with a carved-out crest, and his father's circlet.

Lore: The Flower belongs to the time before the first blood was shed in the feud; the exile, having seen human cruelty, left his gentleness in the past but treasured the faded flower and his old innocent smile. The Feather fell from a panicked bird fleeing a falcon onto his shoulder as he walked alone through plains and forests, a symbol of a nestless free bird like himself. The Pocket Watch recorded his carefree youth, ended by tragedy and long lonely exile. The Goblet is a silver family heirloom whose gem with the family crest he carved out after bringing shame to his family; it is broken and can hold no liquid, yet he carries it. The Circlet recalls a childhood in a silver palace, the father's circlet as a symbol of nobility, and a later feud that painted the collapsing palace blood-red; it became the evidence of the exile's crime.

Owners: The unnamed exile; the wiki identifies him as Parsifal.

Status as of 7.1: The exile is a figure of about a thousand years ago and long dead. Nothing in 6.x or 7.0-7.1 changes this set.

571.content: The Exile is the unnamed aristocrat of the Exile set texts, a noble who fled after a bloody family feud, carved his crest out of his heirloom goblet and wandered with a broken cup and a blue feather. The wiki ties him to Parsifal.

key: The Fall of the Faded Castle
572.comment: The Fall of the Faded Castle
572.content:
The Fall of the Faded Castle (also: Fall of the Faded Castle (poem)): The poem is anonymous and names no one. Its images (a castle by the purest lake, a master haunted by midnight, a dark ancient world, a blood moon) match the story of the Faded Castle in the Nostoi Region, but the book itself never says so. Treat it as an in-world ominous poem whose literal truth is not confirmed.

Appearance: A 3-star book collection of three volumes. Vol. 1 lies inside The Rusty Rudder next to the entrance. Vols. 2 and 3 are sold by Hubel. The cover title is written in the Fontaine Script.

Lore: Vol. 2: by the shore of the world's purest lake stood a glittering castle, with gold leaf and gems on its walls, banners, towers, colourful windows and odd lifelike statues. A golden stage held musicians who played day and night for the castle's master, and guests of every class and homeland danced and drank. Nothing eased the master's fear. Each time the tower clock struck midnight he was gripped by panic, sure that the dark-robed figure would come to collect a debt and turn everything, including his guests' souls and his own, to dust as tribute to a dark ancient world.

Vol. 3: the castle falls quiet, with sounds of animals chewing and a rasping laugh from an empty room. A glowing red fog and storm wrap the castle, a tall thin figure in black robes appears on the central stage, and guests fall one by one without time to scream. The master's soul is taken on his throne. The castle collapses into the waves and the blood moon its towers had hidden reappears. Today the water reflects the ruin, whose statues look like monsters, and only darkness, death and loss remain.

Owners: No owner. It is a commercial book found around Fontaine.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 3-star Book Collection added in 4.2. Its cover reads "FADED CASTLE" in the Fontaine Script.

key: The Fall of the Faded Castle
573.comment: The Fall of the Faded Castle: The Dark-Robed Figure
573.content: In the poem The Fall of the Faded Castle a tall, slim figure in dark robes appears twice: on a rotten black ship in a dream, and on the castle's stage at midnight to collect a debt and take every soul in the hall. Its nature is left open by the text. Identifying it with the Faded Castle's real fall is an inference.

574.content:
The First Great Magic: The First Great Magic is a 5-star bow: a stage prop once used by a past Great Magician, whose final secret was that it was also a weapon beyond the pale.

Its story is the rise of the magician Parsifal the Great and her assistant Josephine, two sisters from the Fleuve Cendre undercity, and what became of the name.

Appearance: Canon only mentions a gem shaped like a cat above the grip, which glows with Pneuma or Ousia when an Arkhe-aligned character holds it. The magician's patter mentions a hat leading to a legendary eastern paradise and a mirror showing peril, as stage props, not as parts of the bow.

Lore: Parsifal the Great is the stage name of a Fontainian woman from the Fleuve Cendre, who performed with her sister Josephine as assistant. The name came from a thief in Master Coppelius's play, which the text calls an elusive thief who appears and disappears at will.

The pair, two young thieves who cheated and stole at the opera house, were dazzled by the knight-errant comedies onstage and forgot why they had come. They began performing in taverns, beside the sewers and at food stalls, then in the spotlight of the grand theatre. Their acts include Feathers into Butterflies, Paradise, Fire in the Mirror and The Golden Fish. The name Parsifal became the talk of both the city above and the city below.

Owners: A past Great Magician, Parsifal, per the description.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star bow, base ATK 46 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT DMG; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 4.0. Passive "Parsifal the Great": raises Charged Attack DMG. Each party member sharing the wielder's Elemental Type (the wielder included) gives 1 Gimmick stack, raising ATK at 1, 2 and 3 or more stacks; each member of another type gives a Theatrics stack, raising Movement SPD. Values scale with refinement. Because the wielder always counts, 1 Gimmick stack is the minimum.

575.comment: The First Great Magic: Parsifal and Josephine
575.content: Parsifal the Great and her assistant Josephine were sisters from the Fleuve Cendre who became the most famous magic duo in Fontaine, per the weapon story of The First Great Magic. Their birth names are unknown. After the Siege of Poisson, a Parsifal asked for trial by combat.

576.content:
The Flute (also: Flute sword): The Flute is a four-star sword of the Wanderer's Troupe series. It has a nimble, delicately engraved and perforated blade that sounded like a flute when swung with skill, the pitch depending on the swing angle. It is tied to a swordswoman of the Troupe later called the Dawnlight Swordswoman.

Appearance: Item text: a thin blade with holes and delicate engraving, lavishly decorated beneath a rusty exterior. After the Troupe disbanded it was buried; unearthed years later it can no longer sing, though it remains lethal.

Lore: Among the Wanderer's Troupe was a valiant sword-wielding dancer. After the Troupe's attempt to tear down the ruling class failed she was enslaved as a gladiator, and though she lost her hope and companions she fought bravely, her sword singing with the morning light; she was dubbed the Dawnlight Swordswoman.

Owners: The Troupe's sword-wielding dancer, later the Dawnlight Swordswoman. The sword was buried when the Troupe disbanded.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Wanderer's Troupe-series four-star sword, base ATK 42, ATK 9% secondary, passive 'Chord' (stacking harmonics). Standard and event wishes.

577.content:
The Folio of Foliage (also: Folio of Foliage): The Folio of Foliage is a three-volume devotional biography of the Dendro Archon during the Cataclysm, kept in the House of Daena in Sumeru. Its text and subject were rewritten after the Archon Quest Where the Boat of Consciousness Lies (3.2).

The narrator, who gives the name Sunitha Cosamvi, says they only wrote down what sages who followed the Archon told them. It reads as scripture, a follower's hymn, not an eyewitness record.

Lore: She weeps as a black tide of decay swallows the world, walks through a ruined forest that blooms under her feet, and goes into the broken heart of the desert to heal it.

Vol. 1: after the moon's shadow shattered, beasts from the abyss devoured the living and the sages named the flood of decay the Black Tide. Her tears gave birth to blossoms full of sweet dew, and she vowed to save the creatures of the earth. Vol. 2: lotuses bloom in her wake, her singing quiets hurricanes, and she goes down alone into the hollowed heart of the land. Vol. 3: few ever heard or recognised her voice; the lord of all animals died protecting what she entrusted to him, and she left the dreamers a promise.

578.comment: The Folio of Foliage: The Folio of Foliage
578.content: The Folio of Foliage is a three-volume devotional biography of the Dendro Archon during the Cataclysm, narrated by a follower who gives the name Sunitha Cosamvi. It describes her tears healing scorched earth, her flowering walk through a ruined forest, and her descent into the hollow heart of the desert to become the earth itself, in the first edition, or to cleanse it and return, after the Irminsul edit of 3.2. The books are found in the House of Daena.

key: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea
579.comment: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea
579.content:
The Fox in the Dandelion Sea (also: Fox in the Dandelion Sea, Foxtale): The Fox in the Dandelion Sea is an 11-part Mondstadt fairy tale told by a hunter. He spares a fox trapped by a Mist Flower, is led to a boundless sea of dandelions, and teaches the fox's child to speak the human tongue in return for the promise of transformation magic. The promise ends with him turned into a dandelion and blown home, and he wakes at the same lake.

Fantasy and folklore, not history; the dandelions, wind wishes and the Anemo Archon fit Mondstadt's folk imagery.

Appearance: Eleven slim volumes with the cover text Foxtale in the Teyvat script. The blurbs repeat the little fox's chant, "Dandelion, dandelion, ride the wind to a faraway land."

Lore: A hunter near a village finds a white fox with its tail frozen in the ice by a Mist Flower and plans to turn it into stew, but its lake-like eyes make his arrow miss and the fox flees. That night the fox returns, becomes a tall black-haired woman and offers thanks. Days later she leads him through a storm of dandelion seeds to a sea of dandelions and asks him to teach her child human language in return for fox magic.

- The hunter learns that foxes who vanish during hunts hide in the dandelion sea. He teaches the little fox language and ordinary skills; the fox wants to become human to befriend a wolf-eyed boy in grey who once drove monsters off.
- The little fox makes a wish to the Anemo Archon by blowing a dandelion, to befriend his teacher. The mother notes the effort of teaching a fox.
- The hunter wants transformation to fly like a falcon, see far places and hunt with magic. As the tale goes on he begins to dread that he will be sent away once lessons end.
- The little fox leaves for the human world, blending into the dandelions. The mother then grows enormous and changes the hunter into a dandelion.
- She chants the same wish, blows the seeds, and he is carried away. A line asks the Anemo Archon to turn foxes into humans so they can be safe from hunters. The hunter wakes in the woods behind his village by the same lake, as if he had dozed off.

Owners: No individual owner; volumes sit in places like Mondstadt Library, Dawn Winery and a table near the Good Hunter, with Vol. 1 given by Flora.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible 11-volume book set; lore only.

580.comment: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea: The Dandelion Wish Chant
580.content: In The Fox in the Dandelion Sea, the little fox blows a dandelion and chants "Dandelion, dandelion, ride the wind to a faraway land," asking that wishes reach the Anemo Archon. It is a fairy-tale device, not a documented Mondstadt ritual.

581.comment: The Fox in the Dandelion Sea: The Hunter and the Fox Mother
581.content: The tale's hunter is nameless. The fox mother thanks him for freeing her from the Mist Flower ice, then asks him to teach her child human speech in return for transformation magic. In the end she turns him into a dandelion and sends him home on the wind.

582.content:
The Legend of Vennessa (also: Legend of Vennessa): The Legend of Vennessa is a two-volume ballad collection popular since Mondstadt's reconstruction. It tells how Vennessa, a fire-haired woman enslaved under the aristocrats, prayed for freedom, was answered by the Anemo Archon Barbatos, and went on to defeat the drake and break the rulers' tower. She is remembered as the founder of the Knights of Favonius.

The song is addressed to a drinking crowd and ends by urging listeners never to give up the pursuit of freedom, even in dark times.

Appearance: Two short verse books written as a bard's performance, opening with a toast to freedom, the Anemo Archon and Vennessa, called the first Knight. The tone is festive and rhymed.

Lore: Vol. 1 sets the scene of old Mondstadt as a dungeon under royal chains, where festivities were the rich's vanity games. It introduces Vennessa as a fiery-headed woman from the southern plains, born free but imprisoned, who still prayed for her people and Mondstadt. Vol. 2 tells that Barbatos descended to her, said every being deserves a name and offered friendship; she marched to battle to his singing, the demonic dragon fled, and the aristocrats cowered.

- The Vol. 1 description says it covers her early years as a slave in Mondstadt. The bard says the Archon's gift was not freedom itself but defiance.
- In Vol. 2 Barbatos says he seeks only her friendship. When she wants to thank him, he answers that she acted first and his songs came to praise her freedom.
- Forest breezes converge and the tyrant's tower is overthrown from the sky; the song calls her a young lioness standing free in the winds.
- The bard closes by telling listeners to remember the dame with the flaming hair when days turn dark.

Owners: No individual owner; copies are in the Grand Master's office at the Knights of Favonius Headquarters, and given by Dr. Edith (Windrise) and Sayid (the Anemo Archon statue plaza, daytime).

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible two-volume book collection; reading is purely lore. A Genius Invokation TCG card of the same name also exists and is a separate item.

583.comment: The Legend of Vennessa: Vennessa's Song and Barbatos
583.content: In the song, Barbatos answers Vennessa's prayer, tells her every being deserves a name, offers friendship and weaves her name into a song. She then fights for Mondstadt's freedom to his singing.

key: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire
584.comment: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire
584.content:
The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire (also: Legends of Reed Miller, Reed Miller pulp stories): Each volume is a different kind of tale: a serial caper in an inexpensive weekly magazine, a romance set around the governor's palace, and a cautionary adventure about a sailor on Miller's ship. All depict Miller as a gifted thief and master of disguise who steals from the corrupt.

Appearance: A 3-star book collection of three volumes, all sold by Dhabit at Mimisbrunnr Books in Nasha Town. Vol. 1 reproduces a cheap magazine serial and has its middle section torn out.

Lore: Vol. 1 details: the editor's note says the serial dwells on the young women pursuing Miller. In Chapter IV, Wagtail, known as "A" to a few, fails to steal his heart. In Chapter XVII Miller says he keeps nothing, and Wagtail remarks that he has stolen the heart of the Frost Moon's daughter.

Vol. 2: A romance about the governor's adopted daughter, Leonita Prokhorovna Trubetskoy, who is nearly of age to be betrothed. Miller announces in the paper that her father Lord Trubetskoy's treasure will be his. Disguised as a footman, he and fellow Treasure Hoarders prepare, after working out that the Sampo Mill, a relic said to produce endless riches, is in the palace. At her birthday ball Leonita learns that she, not the governor, is the true source of the wealth, and that her "treatments" were rituals. Miller reveals himself and says that she, not the Mill, is the treasure he came for. The narrator ends by saying she left to travel the world with him.

Vol. 3: Zima, a young man from a village near Snezhnograd, leaves Snezhnaya to avoid a predictable fate after seeing a friend turned into a statue by a Snegurochka. He joins Miller's ship, expecting adventure, and finds Miller careful and cautious about monsters. A siren demands a sacrifice. When tossed Mora fails to pay, Miller puts a scimitar to Zima's throat. Zima realises that his flight from patterns was only another pattern.

Owners: No owner. It is a commercial book sold in Nasha Town.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 3-star Book Collection added in 6.0, bought from Dhabit at Mimisbrunnr Books.

585.comment: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire: Sampo Mill (in the pulp stories)
585.content: In The Legends of Reed Miller the Sampo Mill is a relic said to generate endless riches, stolen from the Frostmoon Scions and hidden in the governor's palace. Vol. 1 has Miller return it, and Vol. 2 claims it works through the silvery-white power of the governor's adopted daughter. These details come from pulp fiction and are not confirmed canon.

586.comment: The Legends of Reed Miller, Thief Extraordinaire: Zima
586.content: Zima is the viewpoint sailor of Vol. 3. He is from a village of ice harvesters southeast of Snezhnograd, joins Reed Miller's ship, and is offered to a siren. He is a character of the pulp story, and the text says nothing more is known of him.

key: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire
Little Witch and the Undying Fire
587.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire
587.content:
The Little Witch and the Undying Fire (also: Little Witch and the Undying Fire): The Little Witch and the Undying Fire is a seven-volume storybook written in turns by members of the Hexenzirkel, the circle of long-lived witches. It follows a young witch who draws the exam topic 'find the undying fire', travels through odd adventures, and finally finds it in an old, dying witch who is the last star still burning. It is a jokey fable that turns into an elegy.

The authorship is mixed on purpose: each volume has its own voice, and the authors' scribbled comments in the volume descriptions are part of the joke. In the Durin story quest (6.2) Alice says it began as a game at the witches' tea parties and that the final volume was left unfinished.

Appearance: A beautifully bound set whose pages are all handwritten. The Vol. 1 and Vol. 7 descriptions note several different hands. Margin comments from the authors tease one another over padding, tangents and unresolved plot threads.

Lore: Vol. 1: a young witch draws the exam topic 'find the undying fire'. Vol. 2: under a blood-green moon she meets a fortune teller and watches the witches' forbidden Night Carnival. Vols. 3 and 4: she hunts and captures demon kings. Vol. 5 (one line): her teacher says the trial is over. Vol. 6: Octavia says the cosmos is dying and the fire exists. Vol. 7: at the end of the universe the old witch is the last star burning, and the little witch carries her flame home.

Notable beats: the fortune teller's contract through the Night Carnival's embers and her gift of a crystal ball (Vol. 2); the mimic and chipmunk demon kings (Vol. 3); the Nephilim and the captured demon king's diplomacy (Vol. 4); Octavia's chair speech (Vol. 6).

Owners: No individual owner. The volumes are collectible books found in the Theater Lobby, per the wiki. Alice is the member who speaks about the book in the Durin story quest.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible book collection with seven volumes added in version 4.7. Reading is purely lore.

588.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire: The Undying Fire and the Star of Scorpio
588.content: In the fable the 'undying fire' is first a mystery set as an exam topic and later the last star still alight at the end of the universe, called the Star of Scorpio and personified as an ancient witch whose flame has dwindled to an ember. The little witch takes the flame home rather than leaving it to die.

589.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire: The Blood-Green Moon and the Night Carnival
589.content: In Vol. 2 the blood-green moon is explained as a symbol of great change whose result cannot be called good or ill, and as the colour of Nephilim blood. The same night is the witches' forbidden Night Carnival, a bonfire rite; the little witch and a fortune teller hide in the trees, and the embers left by the fire serve as the contract offering to a witch.

590.comment: The Little Witch and the Undying Fire: The Authors of the Fable
590.content: Seven Hexenzirkel members took turns writing it, per the wiki's reading of Durin's character story. Alice says it began as a tea-party game. The final volume was meant for another member, 'M', who died; Alice wrote an ending on her behalf.

591.content:
The Mondstadt Tower (also: Mond Tower novel): The Mondstadt Tower is a one-volume historical romance novel set in the dark age of Mondstadt's aristocrats. Its blurb promises a fateful meeting between an outlander girl and an ominous orphan. The text that survives in-game follows the singer Ines, who throws the Harpastum at Ludi Harpastum, and the Seneschal and his adopted son Octave.

It is fiction, so use it for the mood and imagination of old Mondstadt and not as a source of confirmed history.

Appearance: A short novel whose cover and spine read Mond Tower in the Teyvat script. Its blurb reads like a serial teaser.

Lore: In the time of the aristocrats a high tower stood in Mondstadt's plaza. It was nominally built to honour Barbatos but was really a show of wealth. The one comfort of the commoners was Ludi Harpastum. At one festival a wandering singer from a distant land, Ines, was admired for her beauty and her songs, and she gave her festival earnings to the poor and orphans. The frail Seneschal fell for her at first sight, but his piety and the Church's claim to aid the poor made him angry, and he plotted to confine her in the Cathedral.

- The novel's setting: the Anemo Archon sleeps, the nobles tyrannise, commoners are poor and the dragon ravages the city. The self-proclaimed orthodox church is a figurehead controlled by the ruling class, preaches abstinence, and even restricts the wind harp to approved holy songs.
- The text says that the idea of divine punishment was an excuse made up by the nobles to hide their greed and restrict the commoners.
- By tradition the maiden chosen to throw the Harpastum serves three days at the royal court under the aristocrats' protection. The Seneschal sends his adopted son Octave to sneak into the court and bring Ines to him quietly, without using the Seneschal's name.
- Octave was abandoned at birth by superstitious parents and was persecuted by townsfolk as a bad omen of draconic disaster. The Seneschal alone protected him, so Octave trusts him fully.
- At nightfall Octave climbs to the court balcony and sees the girl weeping in the moonlight. He forgets his task, until servants interrupt them, where the text ends.

Owners: No individual owner; a copy is in the Grand Master's office, and Patchi the Curious gives one at the Thousand Winds Temple.

Gameplay: Game note: a collectible book; reading is lore only.

592.comment: The Mondstadt Tower: Octave and the Seneschal
592.content: In the novel The Mondstadt Tower, Octave is the Seneschal's adopted son, an abandoned child persecuted as a bad omen, who trusts the one man who protected him. The Seneschal sends him to fetch the singer Ines. Both are fictional characters of the novel.

key: The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies
Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies
593.comment: The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies
593.content:
The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies (also: Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies, Pale Princess and Six Pygmies): Its title echoes the German fairy tale Snow White (wiki trivia, an out-of-world observation). The Abyss Order's interest in a 'secret' inside it is never explained.

Appearance: A 4-star Book Collection of seven installments. Vol. 1 is received directly from a quest, unlike most books, which are found in the world or bought.

Lore: The Night Mother is called the source of all sins, with neither heart nor mouth, always watching and punishing unpredictably. The one thing she could not bear was moonlight breaking through the clouds. The Moonlight Forest kingdom lived in that moonlight; the tale suggests their beauty came from it, in contrast to the abhorrent creatures at the forest edge.

Owners: Held by the Mondstadt library under Lisa as librarian. After Lost Book, the Traveler is registered as its custodian rather than borrower, a privilege Lisa says is reserved for trusted citizens, with no due date.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Vol. 1 is an automatic reward at the end of Lost Book (the second half of Troublesome Work).

594.comment: The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies: Lost Book (stolen library copy)
594.content: In the Mondstadt story quest Lost Book (Tempus Fugit Chapter, Act I), Lisa asks the Traveler to help recover a borrowed library book whose copy of The Pale Princess and the Six Pygmies has been stolen. Following her elemental marks near Starfell Valley leads to a hidden Abyss Mage stronghold. Lisa defeats the mage, who says the book holds a secret, and the book is found in a chest below. Lisa and Paimon judge it an ordinary storybook.

595.content:
The Saga of Hamavaran (also: Saga of Hamavaran, Hamavaran Saga): The Saga of Hamavaran is a three-volume light novel by the writer Pursina, sold at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City. It follows a Sumeru scholar named Hamavaran who travels to Inazuma.

Vol. 1 is a publisher's foreword, Vol. 2 opens the comic story of Hamavaran's voyage and Vol. 3 introduces his talkative companion, a shikigami who calls herself a "ghost-calling".

Appearance: Three slim novel volumes, with the first collecting the prefaces of the new light novel into its own volume due to "a business model adjustment". The cover is written in the Inazuman script and reads LGDHMVR, which the wiki takes to stand for "Legend of Hamavaran".

Lore: The foreword thanks writers drawn in by a recruitment drive and a contest called "This Novel is Amazing!", and thanks Kanjou Commissioner Hiiragi Shinsuke. It says that before the Sakoku Decree accomplished samurai from many lands lived in Inazuma, among them Hamavaran from the rainforest nation of Sumeru, whose tale was buried under the Shogun's eternity and is now retold by the budding author Pursina.

596.comment: The Saga of Hamavaran: The Saga of Hamavaran
596.content: The Saga of Hamavaran is a light novel by Pursina sold at the Yae Publishing House. Its hero is Hamavaran, a Sumeru scholar of marine biology who sails to Inazuma, meets a shikigami who calls herself a "ghost-calling", and compares her to Sumeru's spirit-warding. The foreword claims Hamavaran was a foreign samurai active before the Sakoku Decree.

597.content:
The Stringless (also: Stringless harp bow): The Stringless is a four-star bow of the Wanderer's Troupe series: an exquisite stringed instrument that is also a bow, once played by the Troupe's harpist from Fontaine. After the Troupe disbanded its harp strings were cut, leaving only the bowstring.

Appearance: Item text: strings of different materials on every section, each trembling to make flowing music when struck. After the Troupe disbanded the strings were cut with a dull blade, creating ear-piercing noise; the lofty melodies are lost but the bow stays deadly. Per the wiki, the Resolution of Sojourner set says it once had four strings.

Lore: The Troupe could make birds fall from the sky, sometimes with the harp's tune and sometimes with the arrows that followed it. The harpist (the Sojourner) was playful and determined, like the wind and the flowers of Starsnatch Cliff. After the failed uprising the Troupe fled, but he stayed to the end, playing and loosing arrows to protect his comrades until his repertoire and arrows ran out.

Owners: The Troupe's harpist (the Sojourner).

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Wanderer's Troupe-series four-star bow, base ATK 42, Elemental Mastery 36, passive 'Arrowless Song'. Standard and event wishes.

598.content:
The Tale of Kuntur (also: Tale of Kuntur): In the tale every tribe child is bound to a Saurian companion. Kuntur's stubbornness and honesty, not any special gift, carry the story. The narrator is a storyteller who comments on events and says "we do not know" about some details.

Appearance: A one-volume Book Collection, listed with no quality rating. It is a reward of the Hidden Exploration Objective Kuntur's Pursuit (the wiki marks that name as unofficial) in Malinalco Grotto, Quahuacan Cliff. The wiki notes that its cover matches its prequel.

Lore: The tribe neither banished nor welcomed father and son, fearing the sun's anger. Kuntur grew up small, sickly and pale, with starry eyes like his mother's, and children who mocked him were answered with his fists. He reached Rumi, freed the Saurians, and let a captive Iktomisaurus go rather than force it to help him. Rumi had visited as a ragged old guest, and the tribespeople fed him until they ran out of patience and sent him away. Only Kuntur refused him, saying he had nothing to give. Rumi then bewitched the hosts and led away their Saurians. The tribe's three best warriors were turned into talking Pakpakas, who tried to trick Kuntur with the same lies that had defeated them. His father's lesson against deceit let him see through them. Rumi's fog failed because Kuntur navigated by sound and smell, learned from his blind father. After Rumi turned to smoke and fled, the bravest freed Iktomisaurus returned on its own, showed him the path, and the pair chased Rumi through animal forms.

Owners: No owner. It is a collectible book obtained in a hidden exploration objective.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a Book Collection added in 5.2, obtained from Kuntur's Pursuit in Malinalco Grotto, Quahuacan Cliff. The wiki notes that kuntur means "condor" and rumi means "stone" in Quechua, and that "Pakpaka" may derive from a Philippine word for "wing"; these are real-world etymologies, not canon.

599.content: In the folk tale The Tale of Kuntur, Kuntur is the son of the star-child Qoyllor and the hunter Ukuku. Disliked because the sun withdrew from his father, he was nicknamed "Kuntur, Unloved of the Sun". He defeated the sorcerer Rumi using his father's hunting skills, his honesty and his persistence, and won an Iktomisaurus companion. He is a story figure with no known counterpart in other canon.

600.comment: The Tale of Kuntur: Rumi the Sorcerer
600.content: In The Tale of Kuntur, Rumi is an infamous sorcerer who disguises himself as a hungry beggar, takes the tribe's Saurians by enchantment and turns three warriors into Pakpakas. He relies on fog, illusions, lies and shapeshifting, and ends frozen solid as a rock above the clouds. He appears only in this folk tale.

key: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku
601.comment: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku
601.content:
The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku (also: Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku): The in-game description calls it a long-standing tale with no knowable original author. It is the first part of a pair; its sequel is The Tale of Kuntur, about their son. The narrator addresses the listener directly in the manner of a storyteller.

Appearance: A one-volume Book Collection. The wiki records no quality rating for it. It is obtained by talking to Orqo during To Wish Upon a Star.

Lore: Qoyllor lived on the star nearest the tribes and was curious about them. After wandering alone she met Ukuku, and they later formed a family, though he grew ever more gloomy. When she learned he had found shards and hidden them because he did not want to lose her, she left in anger and sadness. The Sun brought her back to the sky and blinded Ukuku with golden arrows; the sun now hides behind clouds wherever he goes. More details: Qoyllor lived on the star nearest the tribes and was far from her brothers and sisters. Over years of travel with Ukuku she learned the life of the ground: she hunted and rested with Saurians, told stories to the tribe's children, ate Tatacos and chased Monetoo. Her cheerful nature let her accept what could not be helped. Doubt came through their neighbour Pochica, who was jealous and who had never got along with Ukuku. He spoke ill of Ukuku to her for years, claiming he clipped the wings of birds he liked and caged them. Pressed by her questions, Ukuku confessed. She demanded the shards, he refused, hoping to keep her, and she left the tribe.

Owners: No owner. It is a collectible book obtained in a quest.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a Book Collection obtained after talking to Orqo in To Wish Upon a Star. The wiki's trivia notes that "quyllur" means "star" in Quechua and that ukukus in Quechua mythology are half-man, half-bear creatures; these are real-world notes, not canon.

602.comment: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku: Qoyllor
602.content: In the folk tale The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku, Qoyllor is a star-child, daughter of the Sun, who fell to the ground and lost the power he gave her. She was cheerful and curious, built a life among a Natlan tribe, and left when she learned Ukuku had hidden shards of her star. Her Sun-father brought her back to the sky. She is a figure of the story and not a known historical person.

603.comment: The Tale of Qoyllor and Ukuku: Ukuku
603.content: In the tale, Ukuku is a strong, taciturn hunter of the tribe, skilled at the chase and at tracking. He promised to help Qoyllor and then hid the shards he found because he had fallen in love with her. As punishment the Sun blinded him with golden arrows, and the sun withdraws behind clouds wherever he goes. He raises their son Kuntur alone in The Tale of Kuntur, where he still hunts despite his blindness.

key: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin
604.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin
604.content:
The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin (also: Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin, Shiruyeh and Shirin): The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin is a two-volume story told by a Jinni in a magic bottle to the shepherd she calls Raven, found in the House of Daena. It tells how the hero Kisra Parvezravan became king of Gurabad, how his father-in-law's line died in one night, and how his son Shiruyeh killed him.

It is a sequel to the quest item The Shepherd and the Magic Bottle, with the same two travellers crossing the desert. The Jinni says it is the spirits' version, and later quests tell the fall of Gurabad differently.

Appearance: Two chapters of dialogue and long speeches by the Jinni, interrupted by camp and desert scenes: sunset over dunes, the sumpter beast, the youth watching the moon. The in-game description calls it a story of unknown origin, full of absurdities.

Lore: Vol. 1: the Jinni explains that in the lost language "Shiruyeh" means "unweaned lion cub", though in the shepherd's tribe it is a branded disgrace. The orphan Kisra, raised in the nest of the giant bird Ghoghnus, becomes the champion of the vassal king Ormazd Shah, destroying ninety-nine cities, tribes and star-sages, and is rewarded with a new name, Parvez, and Ormazd's daughter Shirin. One night Ormazd and all 300 of his offspring die in Gurabad, and Kisra, now Parvezravan, takes the throne.

Vol. 2: Shirin is the daughter of Ormazd and the fairy Liloufar, whose prophecies tell of a hero husband, a sweet end to many relatives and Shirin alone inheriting the kingdom. Slaves, mages of the Mazandaran Oasis or Fellahin servants poison the banquet; only Shirin, shut out by her father, and her husband Kisra keep their lives. Parvezravan banishes their son Shiruyeh in a mask, and Shirin disguises herself, urging him to confront the coward on the throne. Shiruyeh stabs his father in bed, is crowned and later falls into a chasm from which Shiruyeh's Plague emerges. Shirin is freed to roam as a haunting spirit, or is said to have been bottled by Al-Ahmar.

605.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin: Shiruyeh
605.content: In The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin, Shiruyeh is the son of Kisra Parvezravan and Shirin, banished masked from Gurabad, who kills his father in his bed, takes the throne, is haunted by nightmares and falls into a chasm. The plague that emerges from it is called Shiruyeh's Plague. In the lost language the name means "unweaned lion cub", while in the shepherd's tribe it is a disgraceful name branded on exiled chiefs.

606.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin: Kisra Parvezravan
606.content: In this tale Kisra is an orphan raised in the nest of the bird Ghoghnus, adopted by the vassal king Ormazd Shah, and rewarded with the name Parvez and Shirin's hand after conquering ninety-nine cities, tribes and star-sages. After Ormazd and his 300 heirs die in one night, he becomes the king Parvezravan, and is later killed by his son Shiruyeh. The tale hints that some say he was behind the tragedy at Gurabad.

607.comment: The Tale of Shiruyeh and Shirin: Shirin and Liloufar
607.content: In this tale Shirin is the daughter of the vassal king Ormazd and the fairy Liloufar, foremother of the spirits. Liloufar prophesies a hero husband, sweet ends for relatives and Shirin's sole inheritance, which become a curse of waiting. Shirin's marriage to Kisra is unhappy, and hatred grows in her; the tale then has her disguise herself to urge her son Shiruyeh to kill his father and finally freed as a haunting spirit or bottled by Al-Ahmar.

608.content:
The Unforged (also: Sword of No Work, Sword of No Skill): The Unforged is a five-star claymore of the Liyue series, an edgeless blade whose description says it can drive away evil spirits and wicked people. Its item story is a legend of an ancient stone dragon in Liyue, and says the sword was planted as a seal beside the tree that subdued it.

Appearance: Item text calls it an edgeless claymore that seems to possess divine might. The wiki connects the name (Sword of No Work, from the idiom about a heavy sword being edgeless) to the idea of power without showy technique.

Lore: Long ago a dragon lived in Liyue, one of the mountains rather than the sky: an ancient dragon of stone as large as its home. Legend says it slept in Nantianmen, looking like the hills, and its smallest stretch shook the earth. Rex Lapis came before it to stop the quaking. The land then knew a long peace, and he gained another comrade.

The union of dragons, gods and men did not last. The dragon was sealed in the earth, and the Geovishaps that had caused havoc beside it fled to the roots of the mountains for fear of the gods and adepti. As millennia passed, the dragon began to stir again.

Owners: No owner is named. Legend places the sword at the Dragon-Queller as a seal.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore. The passive Golden Majesty raises Shield Strength and stacks ATK on hits, with a larger bonus while shielded. It shares this passive with Memory of Dust. Obtained from Weapon Event Wishes; added in Version 1.1.

609.content:
The Viridescent Hunt: The Viridescent Hunt is a 4-star bow from the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn, in the game since Version 1.0. The in-game short description calls it a pure green hunting bow that once belonged to a hunter whose home was the forest. The full text is the tale of a nameless hunter taught never to loose an arrow for anything but survival.

According to the wiki, the lore of the Viridescent Venerer artifact set ties into this weapon.

Appearance: A bow of a pure green so close to the natural environment that, per the text, it could blend in. No other design details are given.

Lore: The hunter was raised, far from the city, to live by the laws of nature, never bearing ill will and loosing arrows only to survive. She left no traces and comforted wounded beasts until their lives returned to nature.

Her teaching said that those born of the greenery move unimpeded where there is grass and shade, that followers of nature need not fear death, and that at the last ebb of life they head to an endless plain.

Owners: The previous owner is the nameless hunter of the text, a woman raised in the forest far from the city; the wiki links the forest to the Dharma Forest and the city to Sumeru City.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): 4-star bow, base ATK 42, CRIT Rate secondary stat. Passive Verdant Wind: Normal and Aimed Shot hits have a 50% chance to create a Cyclone that draws in nearby opponents, dealing 40 to 80 per cent of ATK (by refinement) every 0.5s for 4s, with a cooldown of 14 to 10 seconds. Obtained through the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn bundle.

610.comment: The Viridescent Hunt: The Nameless Hunter
610.content: The Viridescent Hunt's nameless hunter was taught by the forest to take life only to survive. A calamity and a dying, blind youth stirred thoughts of revenge in her; she asked that the bow remain unstained by it. Her story ties into the Viridescent Venerer artifact set.

key: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins
Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins
611.comment: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins
611.content:
The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins (also: Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins): The narrator tells the tale as a storyteller by a bonfire, skipping parts "less important to the listeners". The scroll is found close to Pacal in the Children of Echoes' territory. The wiki notes that the quest Shadows of the Mountains reveals what really happened.

Appearance: A one-volume woven scroll, quality 4 per the wiki, found near Pacal in the Children of Echoes area.

Lore: The Lord fouled the springs of the People of the Springs with smog, sent sparks to the Scions of the Canopy, and swallowed the Collective of Plenty, who escaped only because Tatankasaurs and warriors breached its stomach while it slept. Wanting the gems of the Children of Echoes' valleys to make its dark belly shine, it was overheard by a flying squirrel; the news passed through an aphid, a rhino and a Tepetlisaurus to Elder Traore, whose Saurian companion that was. The Children's strongest warrior and chief Sundjatta had gone with the hero Tenoch to the island in the far west to stop a giant dark beast, so Traore and the guarding warriors asked their Wayob for aid. The Volcano Lord approached through smoke. At the Sulfurous Veins Traore met it, flattered it, and led it to a stone chamber with a human-sized gate and no room for it, saying it could reach in with its hand. To reassure it he entered first. As the Lord's fist closed around the gems and grew too large for the gate, Traore blew a golden whistle. The warriors in ambush called on the Wayob, which borrowed four sewing pins, three short and one long, and blew them at the Lord. The pins took on the tribe's blood and the Wayob's power and became four huge phlogiston nails. Three pinned the black arm to the Sulfurous Veins, and the Lord severed its own arm and fled before the longest could fall.

Owners: No owner. It is a collectible scroll found in the world.

Gameplay: Gameplay note (not in-world): a 4-star Book Collection added in 5.0, found near Pacal at the Children of Echoes in Natlan. The wiki lists a video guide for locating the series.

612.comment: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins: The Volcano Lord
612.content: In the legend The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins, the Volcano Lord is a dark giant like a black-and-purple salamander that seized the Great Volcano of Tollan and harried Natlan's tribes. It was tricked by Elder Traore, lost an arm to the Wayob's phlogiston nails and fled. The wiki links this being with the Abyss, which the scroll itself does not say.

613.comment: The Volcano Lord and the Shadow Pins: Shadow Pins
613.content: In the legend, the Shadow Pins are the long crystalline pillars of the Sulfurous Veins, said to be the phlogiston nails that pinned the Volcano Lord's arm like a shadow. The longest is said to hang suspended, keeping the Lord away from the Children of Echoes. They are a real feature of the area, and the origin story is a legend.

614.content:
The Widsith (also: Widsith notebook): The Widsith is a four-star catalyst of the Wanderer's Troupe series: a heavy notebook of hand-written musical scores and travel journals, moth-eaten and worn, that the Troupe shared. It records their experiences and still carries power drawn from their performances.

Appearance: Item text describes a heavy notebook filled with musical scores, suffering moth damage and wear but with much power in the hand-written words.

Lore: The notebook was passed among the Troupe's members and holds scores and travel journals about the lands they roamed. It siphons power from the records of their performances and the cheering of the crowds. The Troupe's history was lost because it disbanded before Mondstadt was rebuilt.

Owners: Shared by the members of the Wanderer's Troupe; no single owner is named.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Wanderer's Troupe-series four-star catalyst, base ATK 42, CRIT DMG 12% secondary, passive 'Debut' (Recitative/Aria/Interlude buff). Standard and event wishes.

615.content:
Thundering Fury (also: Thundering Fury artifact set, Thunderbird's Mercy, Survivor of Catastrophe, Hourglass of Thunder, Omen of Thunderstorm, Thunder Summoner's Crown): Thundering Fury is an Electro artifact set (4 and 5 star). Its five pieces tell, in fragments, of an ancient tribe that worshipped the Thunderbird, a violet-lightning bird. A young lad who sang to the bird became a blood sacrifice, and the enraged Thunderbird destroyed the tribe. The set is earned in the Midsummer Courtyard domain.

The set's pieces are Thunderbird's Mercy (flower), Survivor of Catastrophe (plume), Hourglass of Thunder (sands), Omen of Thunderstorm (goblet) and Thunder Summoner's Crown (circlet). The tribe is the one now called the Thunderbird Civilization, of Tsurumi Island in Inazuma.

Lore: The tribe feared the Thunderbird and thanked it for its blessings, and shamans offered blood to it for protection and forgiveness. The texts insist the bird was a monster that did not care for human worship, and the tribe took its unpredictable moves for divine revelations.

One stormy season a young lad sang fearlessly in the mountains, and the proud bird landed beside him. He said he had been told he could bring peace to thunder and storms, and the bird, moved by his song, said nothing. That was their only meeting. The next time the bird saw him was as blood in the golden goblet on the sacrificial altar. At the tribe's last festival, where the hourglass counted down to the bird's arrival, the frenzied Thunderbird blew away the altar and destroyed the tribe in vengeance for the singer. The text adds that the lad himself saw his death as an offering for the tribe's good.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 2-piece bonus of +15% Electro DMG. The 4-piece bonus boosts Overloaded, Electro-Charged, Superconduct and Hyperbloom damage by 40% and shortens the Elemental Skill cooldown by 1s when the wearer triggers Quicken or those reactions (once per 0.8s); the set also boosts Aggravate, Lunar-Charged and Stellar-Conduct by 20%. The set drops in the Midsummer Courtyard domain.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): use the set as a grim, quiet relic. Show purple lightning clinging to the pieces, and treat it as a remembered tragedy rather than a trophy. Do not give it to a canon character or make it grant powers.

616.content: Thundering Fury texts describe a tribe on Tsurumi Island that worshipped the Thunderbird and offered blood to it. A singing lad was sacrificed, and the Thunderbird annihilated the tribe in anger. The bird was hunted down and killed years later.

617.content:
Thundering Pulse (also: Rule By Thunder, the Shogun's bow): Thundering Pulse is a five-star bow, a longbow with eternal lightning crackling around it that the game calls a gift from the Shogun. Its item story follows the samurai Takamine the Mistsplitter, who won it from a Great Tengu in a gamble, learned Tengu archery from it, and left it as a wager with a shrine maiden when he went to face the disaster from across the sea. He did not return as himself.

The bow keeps its sheen despite having been soaked in thick darkness, a detail the text uses to mark that it outlasted both the Cataclysm and its owners.

Appearance: The text describes a bow that crackles with thunder and retains its luster even though it was soaked in thick darkness. The game description calls it a longbow with eternal lightning around it.

Lore: When disaster came from a distant sea, the bow was the favourite weapon of a great swordsman, Takamine. In his youth he wandered the mountains and met a great Tengu, with whom he wagered his young, strong body against a bow given by the Shogun. The wager was a draw, three wins each; he became the Tengu's servant but won the bow. The Tengu gave him the ridiculous nickname Konbumaru and showed him Tengu archery, a fierce, unpredictable and elegant form of fighting, loosing thunderbolts with every bowstring's pulse.

Owners: Forged by the Shogun (not specified which one) and given to Reizenbou. Then Takamine the Mistsplitter, who won it in a gamble. Then Asase Hibiki, who received it as a wager prize and is its last known owner. Kujou Sara is depicted with it in artwork, which is not an ownership claim.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star bow from the Inazuma series, base ATK 46, secondary stat CRIT DMG 14.4%. Passive "Rule By Thunder": ATK +20-40%, plus the Thunder Emblem, which gains a stack on each Normal Attack hit (5s) and each Elemental Skill cast (10s) and disappears when Energy is full; stacks 1/2/3 boost Normal Attack DMG by 12/24/40% up to 24/48/80% at refinement 1-5. It was the event-exclusive weapon of the Version 2.0 Epitome Invocation, alongside Skyward Blade.

618.content: Takamine is the great swordsman of the item stories, the one-time servant of the Tengu Reizenbou who won this bow and later owned Mistsplitter Reforged. The Thundering Pulse text gives him the nickname Konbumaru from his time as a Tengu's servant and tells of his wagers. His own entry carries the rest of his story.

619.content:
Thundersoother (also: Thundersoother's Heart, Thundersoother's Plume, Hour of Soothing Thunder, Thundersoother's Goblet, Thundersoother's Diadem, Flower of Thunder): Thundersoother is an Electro artifact set from launch (Midsummer Courtyard domain). Its five pieces recount a legendary hero, "the Thundersoother", who conquered thunder and lightning, killed the tyrannical Beast of Thunder, and later lived and died alone.

The story is told in legend-like fragments with no names, dates or places.

Lore: The Beast of Thunder once enslaved people with its lightning. The Thundersoother, who plucked the purple Flower of Thunder with reverence and wore it on his chest, fought the beast without wavering and defeated it in a lightning storm, beheading it and claiming a diadem as his trophy.

He made tools from amethyst and Electro shards: an insignia shaped like the plume of a falcon that fearlessly crossed storms and a burnt woodland, and an hourglass of Electro shards that shatter and merge as time passes. Watching it taught him about the cycle of life and death, which helped him defeat the beast. His goblet is said to have held the wine for the sacrificial slaying of his family, the courage for entering the beast's cave, and his only company in his last years of solitude.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): 4 and 5 star set from Midsummer Courtyard and its strongbox. 2-piece: Electro RES +40%. 4-piece: +35% DMG against Electro-affected opponents; it does not trigger on the hit that applies Electro, still works off-field, and stacks additively with other DMG bonuses. Introduced in 1.0.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): tell it as an anonymous legend of a solitary, grieving hero. Do not name him or connect him to a nation or to the Thundering Fury set.

620.content: The flower piece: a purple flower that blooms only in thunderstorms and never withers in the rain. The Thundersoother knelt to pluck it and wore it on his chest; for travellers, it gave unfaltering resolve against thunder.

621.content: The plume piece: an amethyst insignia in the shape of a falcon's feather. The falcon left it in burnt woods after flying through storms and volcano; the Thundersoother, like it, conquered both thunder and flame.

622.content: The sands piece: an amethyst hourglass filled with Electro shards that shatter and merge as time passes. The hero learned about the cycle of life and death from it.

623.content: The goblet piece: his cup, said to have held the wine for the sacrificial slaying of his family, the courage for the beast's cave and the only company of his solitary final days.

624.content: The circlet piece: a very ancient diadem that shines with the light of pacified lightning, taken as a trophy from the Beast of Thunder after the storm fight.

625.content:
Tidal Shadow: Tidal Shadow is a four-star claymore of the Beaumont series, forged in Fontaine. The description calls it an exquisitely crafted standard-model sword for the high-ranking officers and flagship captains of Fontaine's old navy. Its story recalls the white ironclad flagship Sponsian and Admiral Basil Elton, whose blue-and-white blade is all that remained of the fleet's legend.

The Navy was disbanded after the armada ceased to exist. The Admiral's First Mate, Nathaniel Pickman, spent his later years trapped by a false heroic reputation.

Appearance: A blue and white blade (the text uses the word epee) of the old Fontaine navy's standard officer pattern. For wielders with Arkhe it shows Pneuma or Ousia alignment indicators.

Lore: In the glorious past the pure white ironclad flagship Sponsian was the pride of Fontaine's Navy, and the Court of Fontaine's darlings were its metal warships with heavy cannons and ramming prows. Basil Elton could be seen on its bridge before her retirement. Afterwards Pickman petitioned the Court for years to salvage and rebuild the Sponsian, but he failed, and the families of the fallen suspected he was fishing for glory.

Owners: Admiral Basil Elton, whose sword the story says it was.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not story. Passive White Cruising Wave raises ATK for 8 seconds after the wielder is healed, and can trigger when the character is off-field. Base ATK 42, ATK 9% secondary stat.

626.content:
Tome of the Eternal Flow (also: Aeon Wave): Tome of the Eternal Flow is a 5-star catalyst: a manual once passed down from generation to generation within an underwater priory. Today none know of its existence.

Its story is the oath of the priory's watchers, who guard the capital of water against a flood and a breach, and the slow decay of the order.

Appearance: Canon gives only that the tip of the tome's spine glows with Pneuma or Ousia when an Arkhe-aligned character holds it. Add nothing else.

Lore: The first watcher led new recruits to recite an oath: remember the oath of a thousand years, defend the foundation of the capital of water, and never forget the sin that was once tempting as honey nor the responsibility that may feel like fetters.
