These shackles stand for the deity's honey-sweet grace and faith in them (the text links the deity to Egeria). The watchers are the shield against the flood, the line of defence against the breach. Those who join have succumbed to the euphoria of violence or to greed; the vow is the recompense of justice and their last chance at redemption. There is neither sunlight nor family, so they must find a semblance of joy.

Owners: No owner is named; it was passed on within the priory.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star catalyst, base ATK 44 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT DMG; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 4.1. Passive "Aeon Wave": raises HP; when current HP increases or decreases, Charged Attack DMG rises for 4s (up to 3 stacks, once per 0.3s); at 3 stacks, or when the third stack refreshes, Energy is restored, once per 12s. Values scale with refinement.

627.comment: Tome of the Eternal Flow: Underwater priory watchers
627.content: In the weapon story of Tome of the Eternal Flow, an underwater priory's watchers, sinners given a second chance by a deity, swear to guard the capital of water against a flood and a breach. The order decays over time, and the last watcher's grave is lost.

628.content:
Toukabou Shigure (also: Toukabou, the cursed parasol): Toukabou Shigure is a four-star sword of the Youkai series, designed as an umbrella and obtained during the Version 3.3 event Akitsu Kimodameshi. Its text is a ghost story ("kaidan") told by a woman from Fontaine: a dancer's cherished umbrella becomes cursed after two deaths, turns into a one-eyed, one-legged, long-tongued youkai, and is finally washed and enshrined by a young shrine maiden.

Appearance: The sword is an umbrella, in the manner of the kasa-obake umbrella youkai. The wiki notes its icon and 3D model are oriented differently from other swords (handle at the bottom left); item text itself describes Inazuman umbrellas in general as exquisite artistry rather than describing this one.

Lore: The narrator is introduced as a visitor who is moved by Inazuman umbrellas. Hundreds of years ago, at a festival season, a girl danced with an intricate umbrella and drank the Oni clan's wine, cheered by humans and youkai alike, until she went to war with the army and died; her subordinates offered the umbrella to a shrine. A martial family's daughter bought it at full price, but before she could use it a message announced her husband's death in battle; she fell ill and died, and her parents returned the umbrella to the shrine to be sealed as cursed.

Owners: No owner is named: the umbrella passes from the dancing girl to a martial family's daughter to a shrine, in an unverified story.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star sword of the Youkai series. Base ATK 42, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 36. Passive "Kaidan: Rainfall Earthbinder": after an attack hits opponents, one of them gains Cursed Parasol for 10s (once per 15s); the wielder deals extra damage to that enemy, and if it is defeated the cooldown refreshes. Obtained during the 3.3 event "Akitsu Kimodameshi".

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a prop for ghost-story nights; keep the "hearsay" framing, and let characters treat it as a spooky tale rather than fact.

key: Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi
629.comment: Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi
629.content:
Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi (also: Shinkageuchi, Chouken Shinkageuchi): Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi is a one-volume traditional Inazuman novel sold at the Yae Publishing House in Inazuma City. Also called "Shinkageuchi", it was once restricted. It tells a fantastical story of the first Shogun and her kagemusha, praising the first Shogun's wisdom and the kagemusha's valor.

It was published in a haphazard way because another book, informally called "Raiden Reincarnation", made readers hungry for this kind of story.

Lore: The book opens with the Goshintou ceremony. When Narukami came to her people she brought the craft of swordmaking; after thousands of years mortal smiths could make swords that pleased her. The Grand Narukami Shrine and the Shogunate therefore gather the finest swords and offer them to the shrine, naming them "Goshintou".

Behind the ceremony, the book says, a master smith never forges just one blade. The finest work, the "Shinuchi", is given a lovely name and offered to the smith's lord or deity; it is not meant to take lives and stays pure. The others, "Kageuchi", go to retainers as weapons, are used in bloodshed and become stained.

Appearance: A single book. According to the wiki, its cover bears the same pattern as the Raiden Shogun's namecard.

Owners: Not a unique item; published for sale by the Yae Publishing House.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a single collectible book sold by Kuroda at the Yae Publishing House. Added in Version 2.2.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's suggestion): use it as a popular, slightly sensational Inazuman novel, and as a source of flavour about Shinuchi and Kageuchi swords. Characters who know the real events (such as Ei) may remark that parts are idealized. Do not claim the novel states the full truth of Makoto and Ei.

630.comment: Treasured Tales of the Chouken Shinkageuchi: Shinuchi and Kageuchi
630.content: In the novel's account of Inazuman swordsmithing, a master smith's finest blade is the Shinuchi, named and offered to a lord or deity and kept pure, while the other blades made at the same time are Kageuchi, given to retainers to use and stained by bloodshed. The novel links the pair of terms to the first Shogun and her shadow sister Ei, and ties it to the Goshintou ceremony.

631.content:
Tulaytullah's Remembrance: Tulaytullah's Remembrance is a 5-star catalyst: a bell of deep sapphire and sterling silver whose echoes are "as crisp as they are distant". Its story recalls the Sapphire City Tulaytullah, home of the Tighnarians, and the farewell of the court dancer Makhaira to her golden-eyed lover Xiphos, and what became of both of them.

The bell's design is based on a ritual bell, the Tibetan drilbu with a vajra handle (wiki trivia on design), which fits the City's ceremonial tone.

Appearance: A catalyst in the form of a sapphire-and-silver bell with a vajra-style handle. The in-game description names only sapphire and sterling silver.

Lore: Once, on the silver dunes, a woman danced with the three sisters of the moon; blood and tears mingled to form a garden spring. The Lord of Flowers grieved, and a sapphire city rose from her tears, where the Tighnarians grew proud and bred generations of wisdom. Tulaytullah was said to be her most precious jewel, and in the golden age even the moon looked amber.

In the gardens bloomed dream-violet Padisarahs and singing pomegranates, and canals shimmered; even passing deities would not see them buried in sandstorms. In a farewell speech Makhaira tells Xiphos, the exiled high-born and Blade of Tulaytullah, beloved of the Jinni, that tomorrow she must leave because the scholars have sold her to the court of Badanah, whose forefathers destroyed her homeland and enslaved her people. She will dance and speak honeyed words among her enemy and asks him to keep her name in his heart for the night.

Owners: No owner is named; the bell is a memory-object of Tulaytullah. Xiphos and Makhaira are the people the story is about.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 5-star catalyst released in Version 3.3 (2022-12-07), level 1 base ATK 48, secondary stat CRIT DMG. Passive Bygone Azure Teardrop raises Normal Attack speed; after the wielder uses an Elemental Skill, Normal Attack DMG increases every second for 14 s and again with each Normal Attack hit (once every 0.3 s), up to a cap. The buff ends when the wielder leaves the field and resets with the next Elemental Skill.

key: Mourning Bell of the Undying One
632.content:
Undying One's Mourning Bell (also: Sigurd's bell, Mourning Bell of the Undying One): The Undying One's Mourning Bell is a bronze bell carried by Sigurd, a Lightkeeper warrior who fought the Wild Hunt in Nod-Krai and, in the item's words, walked through the dark abyss. Its peal is said to be heard on pitch-black nights. The Traveler recovers it as a quest item and returns it to his grave, and it also exists as the Sands piece of the Long Night's Oath artifact set.

Beasts are said to flinch at the sound of Sigurd's warning bell. The Lightkeepers still try to carry on the work he left unfinished.

Appearance: A bronze bell. The item text adds only that it is Sigurd's and that its peal can be heard on pitch-black nights; no further design is described.

Lore: Sigurd was a formidable Lightkeeper who fought the Wild Hunt to the end. The bell is the sound of his stubborn watch: folk tales hold that whenever mournful bells toll, the one who swore to hunt the Wild Hunt is near.

The artifact text describes a terrible storm of black rain and a host of spirits crossing the night sky, which people of the borderlands call the Wild Hunt. A black-feathered flock of crows and an oath-bound legion pushed forward against it. Sigurd, the last one standing with a dark blade, reached the edge of the forest where the Hunt's source lurked, but his body had already been torn apart; the bell he carried kept ringing amid the blood and black muck, and the carrion feeders around him faltered. He was left to walk alone in the abyss to fulfil an oath not yet kept.

Quest use: In The Bell of Mourning Echoes (World Quest, Nod-Krai, Version 6.0), the Traveler and Paimon clear Wild Hunt corruption at Tideseal Stones with a strange, Lightkeeper-clad figure fighting beside them. Cleansing three stones yields this bell, A Horn Unwinded and a Dyed Tassel. Lushne and Sukhovykh in Nasha Town recognise them as Sigurd's.

Owners: Sigurd carried it in life. After the quest the Traveler returns it to his grave; in the artifact system it can be equipped by any character.

Gameplay: Gameplay (labelled): as a quest item it has no use in play. As an artifact it is the Sands of Eon piece of Long Night's Oath, whose 2-piece bonus increases Plunging Attack DMG by 25%.

633.comment: Undying One's Mourning Bell: Undying One's Mourning Bell
633.content: Sigurd's bronze warning bell. Beasts and Wild Hunt creatures are said to flinch at its peal. The Traveler recovers it and two other relics in The Bell of Mourning Echoes and returns them to his grave on Lempo Isle. It is also the Sands piece of the Long Night's Oath artifact set.

634.comment: Undying One's Mourning Bell: The Bell of Mourning Echoes
634.content: A Nod-Krai World Quest begun by collecting Sigurd's relics from three Tideseal Stones. Lushne and Sukhovykh of the Lightkeepers in Nasha Town identify them, and the Traveler lays them at his grave, which triggers the Sigurd Local Legend. Not a Treasure Hoarder or Reed Miller matter; it is about the Lightkeepers' dead.

key: The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched
635.content:
Unfinished Reverie (also: Unfinished Reverie artifact set, Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers, Faded Emerald Tail, Moment of Attainment, The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched, Crownless Crown): Unfinished Reverie is a 4- and 5-star artifact set, added in Version 4.6, whose lore belongs to Natlan. Its pieces tell of the scarlet-eyed youth who gathered heroes against an insane king, and of a young girl, twin heroes, a taciturn warrior and a scarred craftsman who helped him. The final piece shows the girl grown old and erasing the craftsman's name. Its bonuses reward fighting Burning enemies with off-field damage.

The pieces are Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers (flower), Faded Emerald Tail (plume), Moment of Attainment (sands), The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched (goblet) and Crownless Crown (circlet). The set is a Natlan story that was released before Natlan itself, in Version 4.6.

Lore: - Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers: as the tribes' banners faded, a half-man holding a cracked ring played on the throne and ordered that none heed the instructions of the ancestors and first ascended.
- Faded Emerald Tail: the girl, bonded to the youth, searched the city for the renowned craftsman among the nobles and found nothing, until a hooded drunkard at a dilapidated tavern told her the story of the feather ornament.
- Moment of Attainment: researchers puzzle over identical burin marks in the same spot on the sundials in the city's ash.
- The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched: the craftsman told the youth and the heroes how the king of the ineffable city had gathered tribal artisans to dig up huge beast-shaped constructs.
- Crownless Crown: the girl, grown old as the mistress of the mines, had promised a turquoise crown to the craftsman once the ancient kingdom fell.
Each piece has its own entry with its full text.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): the 2-piece bonus is ATK +18%. The 4-piece bonus gives +50% DMG after leaving combat for 3s; in combat the bonus drops by 10% per second after 6s without a nearby Burning opponent, and climbs 10% per second to 50% while a Burning opponent is nearby. It still works if the wearer is off-field.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): present the pieces as bittersweet relics of a rebellion told by those who loved its unsung planner.

636.content: Sakkuk appears as the daughter of the mines who sent wandering spirits back to the night realm and later as the long-lived old mistress of the mines who bought the craftsman's works and erased his name. The wiki identifies her as the first hero to join the scarlet-eyed youth and as a chief of the Children of Echoes.

637.content: In this set the scarlet-eyed youth returns from the kingdom of flowing light to gather heroes against the insane king, summons a god's fiery wrath to burn the corroded city and returns to the sacred flames after completing his calling. Wider canon names him as the second Pyro Archon; the pieces only call him a youth and a hero.

638.content: The twins are described as the elder, whose lips and teeth were sharper than any blade, and the younger, whose back bore the tyrant's lash. Atawallpa rekindled the desire for past glories in Moment of Attainment. A surviving twin mourns him in Crownless Crown.

639.comment: Unfinished Reverie: Dark Fruit of Bright Flowers
639.content: as the tribes' banners faded, a half-man holding a cracked ring played on the throne and ordered that none heed the instructions of the ancestors and first ascended. When darkness seized the depths, a red-eyed youth returned from the kingdom where water flowed as rays of light to the ineffable city. A blind, stooped old woman warned him to seek the truly righteous, those who still stand in the cold night and throw themselves on the fire. A young girl came first, then the hero twins (the elder sharp-tongued, the younger scarred by the tyrant's lash), then a taciturn warrior who hoped Saurians and humans could live in peace. The youth needed someone who knew the city's secret and open paths and could handle mechanisms like toys, and the warrior named a craftsman.

640.content: the girl, bonded to the youth, searched the city for the renowned craftsman among the nobles and found nothing, until a hooded drunkard at a dilapidated tavern told her the story of the feather ornament. He was a beggar whose face was burnt away on one side. She had lost her father, condemned for protecting the tribe's Saurians, and he saw the same hatred in her eyes. He offered his service before she asked.

641.content: researchers puzzle over identical burin marks in the same spot on the sundials in the city's ash. Those who came from the canyons thought it a time to relight the obsidian pillars, and Sakkuk, daughter of the mines, sent wandering spirits back to the night realm. Those from the hanging trees renewed the contract with the Saurians of the six tribes, and Yupanqui shattered the shackles on a Saurian's neck. Those from the spring's source heard again the echoes of the waves, and Atawallpa rekindled the desire for past glories. Those from the mountain peaks returned to freedom, and the scarlet-eyed hero summoned a god's fiery wrath to burn the corroded city and restore the tribe. According to unofficial histories, a skilled artisan with no recorded name planned the overthrow of the insane king, then vanished from the old stories.

key: The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched
642.comment: Unfinished Reverie: The Wine-Flask Over Which the Plan Was Hatched
642.content: the craftsman told the youth and the heroes how the king of the ineffable city had gathered tribal artisans to dig up huge beast-shaped constructs, and burned everything and everyone to bury the secret behind a stone gate. A golden tear from a stone head fell into the craftsman's eye as he lay dying, and he saw the machines, shadows climbing to the moon, golden patterns and an alternate escape route, and the iron laws that built the empire. The twins laughed it off as a tale. He hoped that, once the dust settled, he could design a brilliant imperial wall for the new king.

643.content: the girl, grown old as the mistress of the mines, had promised a turquoise crown to the craftsman once the ancient kingdom fell. After she saw his corpse hunched beneath a black beast's butcher's blade, the crown waited alone for a master who would never attend a coronation. She bought his genuine works and forgeries alike, at any price in gems, so the fakes would not stain his name, and she dealt harshly with cheats. Outliving the youth, who returned to the sacred flames, the warrior who fell into the ruler's flames, and the twins, she took the last of his true works into the dark night and never returned. Next day, the tribes swore beneath the tree where the crown lay to follow her last order, to blot the craftsman's name from history.

644.content:
Uraku Misugiri (also: Misugiri, Brocade Bloom, Shrine Sword): Uraku Misugiri is a five-star sword made by the renowned literato Urakusai, a Kitsune. Legend says that in hundreds of years it has never cut any living creature. The name comes from an episode where a drunken Urakusai sliced the gold-lacquered stage curtains of the bake-danuki in a dance, and the sword was later given as a reward to the man known as the Otogi King, "he of the Front Gate".

The item story adds a second, oral account from the oni: the Otogi King traded the blade to a young tailor for her scissors, and she later wove a scroll of him with two swords.

Appearance: The text calls it a great golden blade, "Misugiri", of famous make. Its owner is pictured in golden brocade threaded with autumn grass and clouds, with painted features; in some scrolls he holds one large and one small sword. The sword's own look is not detailed beyond its name and size.

Lore: Urakusai once earned the bake-danuki's undying enmity by cutting the gold-lacquered stage curtains in the forest during a drunken reverie. That gave his sword its name, and his blade-wild dance under the moon became a tale told by everyone but the bake-danuki. He later apologised to the performers and gave them his tea set and other treasures. The man "of the Front Gate" had met him only once before, and received the blade as a reward for mediating between the parties.

Owners: Maker: Urakusai. Recipient: the Otogi King, "he of the Front Gate". According to the oni account, he gave it to a young tailor of common birth, who is unnamed in the text. The item is an ordinary player weapon in-game.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star sword from the Otogi King series, base ATK 44, secondary stat CRIT DMG 19.2%. Passive "Brocade Bloom, Shrine Sword": Normal Attack DMG +16-32% and Elemental Skill DMG +24-48%; after a nearby active character deals Geo DMG, those bonuses double for 15s; the wielder's DEF rises by 20-40% (refinement 1-5). It was one of two event-exclusive weapons in the Version 4.5 Epitome Invocation (2024-03-13), alongside Redhorn Stonethresher.

645.content: Urakusai is the renowned Kitsune literato who made the blade. The item story shows him as a refined drinker who offended the bake-danuki, made amends, and later grieved for the scattered, wandering people. His own entry carries what else is known.

key: Many Oaths of Dawn and Dusk
646.content:
Verdict (also: Many Oaths of Dawn and Dusk): Verdict is a 5-star claymore of Fontaine, released in Version 4.3 alongside Navia. Its item text tells of Leticia, the eldest daughter of the noble House Randolph, who slipped into the underground Fleuve Cendre in disguise, fell in love with a young man there, and eventually abandoned her family name to live among its people. The weapon is described as stained with the blood of enemies and loved ones alike.

Its passive is named Many Oaths of Dawn and Dusk, echoing the oaths in the story. The weapon's text is one of several Fontaine item stories about the Fleuve Cendre and the events leading to the Siege of Poisson.

Lore: A young noblewoman, Leticia, is told by her father that as the eldest daughter of House Randolph she must keep a composed, pure bearing, because when nobles fall they drag many common homes down with them. She still disguises herself and goes down to the Fleuve Cendre, the sunless subterranean city. A man there sees through the disguise and invites her to see how its people live.

Her guide is a young man she already knows by name; he explains that her father, brother and servants need not learn of this place, quoting the Boss's saying that the sun's light belongs to others and the Fleuve Cendre to them. He later tells her he adores her noble soul and that if he is ever lost, her hand will decide his fate. Years pass; when she meets her father again she has taken on the name of the rose and is used to the weight of an axe rather than fine dresses. She tells him she has made a pact with her beloved and an oath to those she loves, and that she will not let the Randolph name be stained on her account. He answers that he lights a candle for her every day, asks her to come home, says her child is innocent and he will not abandon it, and hints that Randolph influence could be used for her husband too.

Owners: The text names Leticia as the weapon's former user ("a young maiden who forsook her family name"). No present-day character is established as owning the original.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star claymore released 2023-12-20 (Version 4.3) in the weapon event Wish, later also in Chronicled Wishes. Base ATK 48 with CRIT Rate as its secondary stat.

647.content: Leticia is the eldest daughter of House Randolph in Verdict's story, who disguised herself to visit the Fleuve Cendre, fell in love with a man there, and later took on the name of the rose and cut ties with her family. See Verdict's lore for the full account; her possible identity as Rosa Reed is an inference and not stated in the text.

648.content:
Vermillion Hereafter (also: Flowering Life, Feather of Nascent Light, Solar Relic, Moment of the Pact, Thundering Poise): Vermillion Hereafter is a 4- and 5-star artifact set that boosts ATK after an Elemental Burst. Its five pieces (Flowering Life, Feather of Nascent Light, Solar Relic, Moment of the Pact, Thundering Poise) have item text about the Chasm in Liyue: the mountain tribes' plea to a four-armed yaksha, the Millelith soldiers who marched into the abyss, and the battle that ended with the yaksha and many soldiers lost.

Added in version 2.6. The text is legend told by miners and merchants; no one is named, and the set is a companion to the older Tenacity of the Millelith set.

Appearance: Relics of the Chasm story: a small flower given as a memento, a dim eagle feather, an ancient solar timepiece, a crystal-sand wine cup, and a fearsome mask.

Lore: Mountain tribes ask a four-armed yaksha for help; he drinks their wine, promises nothing and goes east into the Chasm, while Millelith soldiers march into the abyss beside him. Both are lost, and the pieces insist the land will remember.

Owners: No owner is named. The pieces speak of a four-armed yaksha, Millelith soldiers and mountain tribespeople, all unnamed.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not lore): obtained from The Lost Valley domain and the Artifact Strongbox. 2-piece: ATK +18%. 4-piece: after an Elemental Burst, the wearer gains Nascent Light (ATK +8% for 16s); each time their HP decreases, ATK rises another 10%, up to 4 times, at most once per 0.8s. It is dispelled when they leave the field, and a new Burst replaces it.

649.content: Artifact set whose item text tells legends of the Chasm: the tribes' plea to a four-armed yaksha, the Millelith's march into the abyss, and the battle in which both fell or vanished.

650.comment: Vermillion Hereafter: The yaksha's pact with the Chasm tribes
650.content: In Moment of the Pact, the mountain tribes' elders offered wine and asked a lone four-armed traveller for help against a shadow troubling the Chasm. He drank it, promised nothing and went east; what followed is left to the listener's knowledge. In Thundering Poise he enters the Chasm with a blade and is lost in the collapse. The text never names him.

651.comment: Vermillion Hereafter: The Millelith soldier's flower
651.content: Flowering Life records a Millelith soldier's farewell to a daughter of the mountain tribe, pledging to follow the four-armed yaksha into the glowing depths. He leaves her a small flower and asks not to be forgotten if he is buried in some nameless place. Neither person is named.

652.content:
Viridescent Venerer (also: In Remembrance of Viridescent Fields, Viridescent Arrow Feather, Viridescent Venerer's Determination, Viridescent Venerer's Vessel, Viridescent Venerer's Diadem): Viridescent Venerer is an Anemo artifact set from launch (Valley of Remembrance domain). Its five pieces tell of a legendary huntress, the "queen of hunters", who moved silently through the forest, stopped hunting animals at a boy's request after disaster struck an ancient kingdom, and hunted monsters instead.

The huntress is nameless apart from her title. The set's story continues in the lore of the bow The Viridescent Hunt.

Lore: In the days when monsters had not yet appeared, the Viridescent Venerer hid her human scent with a white wild flower, and was sought by walking barefoot through the forest. The one who found her was a boy, when disaster had just befallen an ancient kingdom. She had once let the grass and mud tell her what birds and roots perceived, but when the God of the Woods died in the disaster the plants stopped speaking, so she used a wayfinding device. At the boy's request she stopped hunting birds and beasts and hunted the monsters that brought suffering instead.

Her arrows once brought death gently: she stroked her prey so its life force returned to nature, and believed she would meet the departed at an endless hunting ground. But she killed the monster that had slain the boy out of vengeance, and believed that hunting ground was then lost to her. The Chinese text ties this to avenging those the monsters hurt on the boy's behalf. Her vessel held the laughter of a campfire she once overheard; she had forgotten human speech, and even after joining the humans no one heard her say a word or saw her leave a trace.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): 4 and 5 star set from Valley of Remembrance and its strongbox. 2-piece: Anemo DMG Bonus +15%. 4-piece: Swirl DMG +60%, Stellar Swirl +20%; lowers the enemy's RES to the swirled element by 40% for 10s, and Cryo RES too on a Stellar Swirl; same-element debuffs don't stack. Introduced in 1.0.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): portray her as silent, gentle and grieving. Do not name her or the boy, and do not state more about the disaster than the items imply.

653.comment: Viridescent Venerer: In Remembrance of Viridescent Fields
653.content: The flower piece: a white wildflower that once covered the land, worn by the huntress to hide her scent. The silent huntress could be found by walking barefoot through the Dharma Forest following its fragrance; the one who found her was a boy, as the ancient kingdom suffered disaster.

654.content: The plume piece: a falcon feather, once fletching on her arrow. She comforted prey so its life force returned to nature, expecting an endless hunting ground, but believed her vengeful killing of the monster that killed the boy cost her that.

655.content: The sands piece: a wayfinding device that points to prey. She once learned what birds saw from the grass and what roots heard from the mud; after the God of the Woods died, the plants fell silent, and at a boy's request she began hunting monsters.

656.content: The goblet piece: a leakproof water pouch she used to store the laughter of a campfire. She had forgotten human speech; no one ever heard her speak or saw her leave a trace.

657.content: The circlet piece: a bloodless hunter's hat, from folklore of the uncrowned queen of hunters, who held to the rule never to become the foe of the earth and forest. It became a frightful sight for monsters in the crisis that followed.

658.content:
Vivid Notions (also: Falling Rainbow's Wish, Dawn's First Hue, Twilight's Splendor): Vivid Notions is a 5-star catalyst: a trophy of gemstones from the Collective of Plenty and crystals from the Flower-Feather Clan, said to have belonged to a legendary wrestler.

Its story concerns a woman of the Collective of Plenty who stepped into the hero's role when the tribes fell into a succession quarrel.

Appearance: Canon says only that it is a trophy of gemstones and crystals. The story speaks of a hero's prop or mask, which is not the same object; keep to a glittering trophy.

Lore: After the six heroes of the blazing sun had stepped into the night wind, the tribes quarrelled over the empty throne. A girl who had stood silently in Wanjiru's shadow burst into the council chamber and drove a half-broken bone blade into the long table, ending the quarrel.

Fietena, born of the Collective and married into the Flower-Feather Clan, then led the united tribes against the Abyss's black tide.

Owners: The description says the trophy once belonged to a legendary wrestler; the story is about Fietena.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 5-star catalyst, base ATK 48 at level 1, secondary stat CRIT DMG; Weapon Event Wishes; introduced in Version 5.5.

659.content: Falling Rainbow's Wish is the passive of the catalyst Vivid Notions (gameplay): an ATK boost, plus Dawn's First Hue and Twilight's Splendor, which raise Plunging Attack CRIT DMG until the plunge lands.

660.content:
Vortex Vanquisher (also: Guànhóng zhī Shuò, Rainbow-Piercing Lance): Vortex Vanquisher is a five-star polearm of Liyue and the weapon Zhongli is shown with. Its item story is a sailors' legend from the days when ships sailed beside sea monsters: Rex Lapis once wielded a spear that pierced the rainbow and pinned a churning vortex in the middle of the deep sea, and whales and dolphins still gather there to sing.

Folklore adds that the vortex is not dead, only stilled, and that one day it will wake and bring a hurricane. The text asks who then will be able to subdue That Which Lies in the Deep.

Lore: In ancient times Liyue Harbor was not at peace because of creatures from the deep. A great shadow dwelt in the oceanic abyss and used great vortices and whirlpools to smash even the strongest ships and drag prey into the sunless depths. Sailors also told of a divine island, rainbow-clad and fog-shrouded, that rises from the sea with treasure for whoever sets foot on it, though others said the island was itself a monster in torpor.

Owners: The story credits the spear to Rex Lapis (Morax). In play it is Zhongli's weapon; the wiki notes that in some one-time story domains and trials he swaps it for the Staff of Homa, which is presentation only.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a five-star polearm from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 46, secondary stat ATK 10.8%. Passive "Golden Majesty", shared by the Liyue series: Shield Strength +20-40% and scoring hits raises ATK 4-8% for 8 seconds, up to 5 stacks, doubled while under a shield (refinements 1 to 5). A shield-friendly passive suits Zhongli's shielding.

661.content:
Vourukasha's Glow (also: Stamen of Khvarena's Origin, Vibrant Pinion, Ancient Abscission, Feast of Boundless Joy, Heart of Khvarena's Brilliance): Vourukasha's Glow is a Sumeru artifact set (Version 3.6, Molten Iron Fortress domain). Its five pieces trace the Khvarena, a daughter-like shard of life made by the Goddess of Flowers: she is entrusted to the queen of grass and trees, forged into the divine bird Simurgh, and finally shatters into the countless flowers of the Vourukasha Oasis. The set is a farewell, not a chronicle.

Its images are verdant: a pilgrim's flower insignia, a feather alive with leaves, a pure liquid timepiece, a wine goblet that was once full of nectar, and earrings of a hundred flowers. The speakers address a daughter or a friend, never an audience.

Lore: A mother warns her "innocent daughter", the Khvarena, of a faceless nightmare in her dreams and sends her to "another mother", a verdant queen of grass and trees whose light is brighter than her own. The Khvarena will face division and death before becoming immortal, and the lord of sweet dew and the lord of grass and trees will lose their divine forms and be forgotten.

Before the Cataclysm's dark tide, the queen of grass and trees forged the Khvarena into a divine bird to guard the border between birth and death. The bird slept among pines and snow-lotuses until disaster woke her. When the dark tide struck, the former leader of the water realm was slain and her body became a sea of pure dew, the Amrita, which would dry up under the Abyss. To cleanse it the divine bird, Simurgh, shattered her own form. The scattered Khvarena fell upon the water mistress's remains and became a sea of flowers; spirits dwell there, singing of the three mothers (verdure, sweet dew, flowers).

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a 4- and 5-star set from the Molten Iron Fortress domain and the Vourukasha's Glow strongbox. 2-piece: HP +20%. 4-piece: Elemental Skill and Burst DMG +10%; after the wearer takes DMG, that bonus rises by 80% for 5s, up to 5 independent stacks, even off-field. Released in 3.6; no later change is listed.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): the set suits quiet, elegiac scenes about the Vourukasha Oasis. Keep the mothers unnamed unless a character knows the Khvarena story.

662.comment: Vourukasha's Glow: Stamen of Khvarena's Origin
662.content: The flower piece of Vourukasha's Glow: a small flower insignia once worn by pilgrims. A mother tells her daughter, the Khvarena, that she is being sent to another mother, because the speaker dreamed of a faceless nightmare and separated her daughter from her body to hold it off.

663.content: The plume piece: a feather-shaped ornament whose colours shimmer like leaves and flowers. It tells of the night before the sandstorm of tragedy, the dark tide, the queen of grass and trees forging Khvarena into a divine bird, the slain water leader whose body became the Amrita, and Simurgh's decision to shatter her form and cleanse it.

664.content: The sands piece: an ancient timepiece with Khvarena's light and a living pure liquid inside. A friend entrusts a shard of Khvarena to the queen of grass and trees, calling it a drop of light in a sea of dew; later the queen shapes it into Simurgh, whose body hides the sea of flowers.

665.comment: Vourukasha's Glow: Feast of Boundless Joy
665.content: The goblet piece: an opulent wine goblet once full of nectar and honeydew, now empty. After the mistress of the orchard dies, the queen of grass and trees cuts ties with the sea of sand and returns to the rainforest to defend life. The Khvarena of flowers, born of joy, give birth to Simurgh.

666.comment: Vourukasha's Glow: Heart of Khvarena's Brilliance
666.content: The circlet piece: earrings in which the glow of a hundred flowers seems to flow. A speaker mourns a wise friend who died young and meditates on remembrance and oblivion. It tells how the verdant bird Simurgh blossomed into countless Khvarena flowers, which fell on the remains of the Amrita's mistress and became the sea of flowers.

667.content:
Wanderer's Troupe (also: Troupe's Dawnlight, Bard's Arrow Feather, Concert's Final Hour, Wanderer's String-Kettle, Conductor's Top Hat, Wanderer's Troupe artifact set): Wanderer's Troupe is a 4- and 5-star artifact set (1.0) about a troupe of travelling warrior-musicians from about a thousand years ago, who used swords for flutes and bows for harps and played for both friends and foes. They recorded their travels in a book called The Widsith. The wiki connects them to a failed uprising against Mondstadt's aristocracy.

The pieces are Troupe's Dawnlight, Bard's Arrow Feather, Concert's Final Hour, Wanderer's String-Kettle and Conductor's Top Hat.

Lore: Troupe's Dawnlight recalls a charismatic swordswoman whose slashes hummed a tune and whose music and sword were both lethal and beautiful. Bard's Arrow Feather recalls a harpist-archer who lured birds with his harp and shot them down, never looking at the sky; companions said it was a hunter's mercy. Concert's Final Hour is a harp-hourglass played to end shows. Wanderer's String-Kettle plays as water flows out. Conductor's Top Hat recalls a troupe that owned no sheet music, whose conductor held The Widsith to the end.

668.content: The book in which the troupe recorded its travels, since it had no sheet music. The conductor still gripped it after death.

669.content:
Wandering Evenstar: Wandering Evenstar is a 4-star catalyst: originally a device used by researchers to observe and calculate celestial phenomena, which now serves as a conduit and catalyst. Its legend is of a prince who lost his kingdom and wandered into the rainforest.

It belongs to the Tulaytullah series with Makhaira Aquamarine and Xiphos' Moonlight, and was released in Version 3.1 through weapon event Wishes.

Appearance: A researcher's celestial observation device, now a catalyst. The description gives no more detail.

Lore: The tale is set thousands of years ago, after the foolish God-King was buried by sandstorms. The wandering prince, having lost his kingdom, retreated into the rainforest, meaning to conquer new lands but pursued by a huntress with a white bow. Trapped by vine branches in cold moonlight, he heard a tiger growl around him.

Quoted lines say the rainforest trail was so treacherous that mortals could tell the way only by moonlight breaking through leaves. The flickering evening stars lit his way yet lured him into a deadly trap. The huntress drove the intruder away again and again, and with the tiger's roar ordered his expulsion, but did not take his life.

Owners: No owner is named, and no character is recorded wielding it.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star catalyst, level 1 base ATK 42, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 36. Passive Wildling Nightstar: every 10 s the wielder gains a percentage of their Elemental Mastery as ATK for 12 s, with nearby party members gaining 30% of it; it works off-field and stacks across copies.

670.content:
Wavebreaker's Fin (also: Umigozen's naginata, Ayame's naginata): Wavebreaker's Fin is a four-star polearm of the Watatsumi series. Item text calls it the naginata of "Umigozen", a mighty Watatsumi warrior, whose edge flows with the phosphorescence of the deep. Narukami's navies are recorded in the island's music as having quailed before her. It is the only proof that she once tried to change the tides of the world.

Appearance: Item text says only that its edge flows with the phosphorescence of the depths and that it is still sharp.

Lore: The text recalls that the twin Watatsumi shrine maidens sang whalesong that followed the tide into the island's dreams, and that Watatsumi's warriors rested their hopes on them. With nagamaki flashing like a white wave, the army advanced on the other islands, until Omikami's glory and that of his warriors were dimmed by the lightning's glow. Mouun was consumed by a dark storm of crow feathers, the great whale sank, and the vassal ruler, "determined as a child", vanished into a rift in the earth.

Owners: "Umigozen" (Ayame, historical.ayame). No later owner is named.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star polearm. Base ATK 45, secondary stat ATK 3%. Passive "Watatsumi Wavewalker" (shared with Akuoumaru and Mouun's Moon): for every point of the party's combined maximum Energy capacity, the wielder's Elemental Burst DMG rises, up to a cap (the maximum needs about 333 Energy cost in the party, which as of 2.5 could be reached with Yae Miko, Raiden Shogun and two more 80-cost characters). Obtained from weapon event wishes.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): the naginata of a heroine who became legend, whose real end is a matter of competing stories.

671.content: "Umigozen" is the title by which the mighty Watatsumi warrior Ayame is remembered in songs. One legend says she died in a last stand against the tengu warriors; another that she steered her flagship into the Dark Sea at the edge of the world. The item text leaves the question open.

672.content:
Waveriding Whirl (also: Fangs Flying To and Fro, Tupac's boomerang): Waveriding Whirl is a 4-star catalyst from Natlan: a boomerang made from a giant sea serpent's fangs. It was a rare weapon that the giant Tupac called "trusty".

Its story follows Tupac, a Meztli giant with no equal on land, as he sails out to sea in search of a worthy feat.

Appearance: Canon: a boomerang made from the fangs of a giant sea serpent. Do not invent size, colour or markings.

Lore: Tupac of the Meztli towered like a mountain, with a sandstone-like body and a burning heart whose steam nearly hid the sun. In an age of peace, when even the ancient shadow-foe was silent, he was sullen, longing to have been born in the age of Xbalanque's dragon-slaying or among those who fought the Python King.

With no equal on land, he walks into the sea to find the bones of a titanic beast or treasures from times past. A winged dragon exiled by an old king gives him wings for sails; the bones of a whale that once drove back waves become his white boat; the fang of a voracious sea python becomes his weapon, and its flesh a meal to drink with.

Owners: Tupac, the giant of the Meztli, by the text.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): a 4-star catalyst of the Heroes of Natlan series, base ATK 41 at level 1, secondary stat Energy Recharge. Weapon Event Wishes from Version 5.2.

673.comment: Waveriding Whirl: Fangs Flying To and Fro
673.content: Fangs Flying To and Fro is the passive of the catalyst Waveriding Whirl (gameplay): cheaper swimming and a Max HP boost after an Elemental Skill, larger with Hydro party members.

674.content:
Bow (also: Bows, bow users): The Bow is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Bow users fight at long range with quick arrow volleys and aimed shots. A fully charged aimed shot carries the wielder's element, so a bow wielder with a Vision fights as an elemental sniper.

Bow users in the archive include Amber, Venti, Fischl, Tighnari, Yelan and Tartaglia. Bows range from plain hunting recurves to heirlooms of the old Mondstadt nobility and the legendary Amos' Bow.

Appearance: A bow is a drawn ranged weapon, carried slung or held ready, with arrows loosed from a standing or moving stance. Designs differ: the Royal Bow's item text calls it an old royal longbow of Mondstadt's erstwhile rulers whose string is still tight after countless generations. Do not assume every bow looks like a plain wooden hunting bow.

Lore: Item text for the Royal Spear records that in the era of Mondstadt's nobility, bows and polearms were regarded as weapons of commoners and gladiators, and the polearm in particular was disliked by sword-carrying nobles because it could threaten them. A noble family's heirloom bow, such as the Royal Bow, is therefore an exception rather than the norm.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): Bow users make long-range attacks. The Normal Attack chain is 3 to 6 quick shots whose paths are fixed once fired, so they can miss a moving target.

Holding the attack button enters Aiming Mode, where aimed shots fly farther and count as Charged Attacks. For most bow characters an aimed shot becomes fully charged after about 1.5 seconds, deals much more damage and is converted to elemental damage. A shot at an enemy's weak point, such as a Ruin Machine's exposed core or the head of most humanoid enemies, is a guaranteed critical hit with extra knockback and poise damage.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): a bow wielder watches distance and wind, keeps a clear line of sight and prefers to open a fight before the enemy closes in. Keep arrows aimed rather than endless, and remember that moving targets can be missed.

675.content:
Catalyst (also: Catalysts, catalyst users): The Catalyst is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Catalyst users cast magic from range through a focus such as a book or an orb. Both their Normal and Charged Attacks deal elemental damage, so their attacks carry the wielder's own element.

Catalyst users in the archive include Lisa, Klee, Mona, Ningguang, Nahida and Barbara. The Catalyst weapon type should not be confused with the Catalyze elemental reaction, which is a separate topic.

Appearance: Catalysts vary far more in shape than other weapon types: spell books, grimoires, orbs and other charms. The Royal Grimoire's item text, for example, describes a book that once belonged to a royal mage of Mondstadt, holding faithful and comprehensive historical accounts as well as magic spells. A catalyst is a conduit for the wielder's own power, so no particular shape is required.

Lore: The Royal Grimoire (Royal Series, Mondstadt) is described by its text as the book of a royal mage of the old nobility, mixing history with spells. Skyward Atlas, a legendary catalyst, has its own entry.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): all Normal and Charged Attacks of a Catalyst user deal elemental damage, and the element matches the wielder's own Vision or natural element. A Normal Attack chain is usually 3 to 4 ranged elemental attacks.

Normal Attacks come in three styles. Projectile attacks home in on the target and may still hit it out of targeting range, as with Ningguang and Kokomi. Non-projectile attacks hit near-instantly at range, as with Lisa and Sucrose. Fixed-hitbox attacks have a set area around the wielder and can be melee, as with Yae Miko, Nahida and Heizou. Charged Attacks typically cost 50 stamina and release a stronger area attack at the target's location.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): show catalyst casting as concentration through a focus, such as pages turning or an orb glowing in the wielder's element, rather than a physical swing. Reach and style depend on the character, so avoid giving every catalyst user the same spell.

676.content:
Claymore (also: Claymores, greatsword): The Claymore is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Claymores are big two-handed weapons: slower than swords and polearms but heavier per hit, with strong interruption and the ability to break shields and Geo objects.

Claymore users in the archive include Diluc, Razor, Noelle, Beidou, Kinich and Mavuika. In the game's classification the claymore is any large two-handed weapon, not only the greatsword.

Appearance: Claymores are oversized and heavy. Most are greatswords, but the category also includes clubs and two-handed axes. The Royal Greatsword's item text describes an old greatsword of the erstwhile rulers of Mondstadt, made from the finest materials and meant for royals only.

Lore: The wiki notes that the word derives from Scottish Gaelic for great sword, and that only the Favonius Greatsword reasonably resembles a traditional claymore. Legendary claymores with their own files include Wolf's Gravestone.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): Claymores restrict the wielder to slower hits than other melee weapons but deal more damage per hit with higher interruption. A Normal Attack chain is typically 3 to 5 slow, wide, powerful attacks.

Claymores are blunt attacks, so they deal increased damage to Geo objects and certain shields and can trigger Shatter on frozen enemies. A Charged Attack has a short windup and then a rapid chain of strikes that drains stamina continuously, ending with a stronger slash when the player releases, runs out of stamina or reaches the maximum duration.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): a claymore swing is deliberate and committing, so a wielder rarely fights delicately. Show the weight in how they carry it and recover from it.

677.content:
Polearm (also: Polearms): The Polearm is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Polearms are long-reaching melee weapons with fast attacks and moderate damage per hit.

Polearm users in the archive include Xiangling, Zhongli, Xiao and the Raiden Shogun. Under Mondstadt's old nobility the polearm was looked down on as a commoner's weapon.

Appearance: Polearms are spears, lances and similar long-handled weapons. The Royal Spear's item text says it was cherished by a member of the old nobility that governed Mondstadt long ago, has never seen the light of day, and is still incomparably sharp.

Lore: Per the Royal Spear's text, as relayed by the wiki, nobles in Mondstadt's era of nobility regarded the polearm, like the bow, as a weapon of plebeian gladiators and commoners, and sword-wielding nobles disliked it as a possible threat.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): polearms have fast attacks, long forward reach and moderate damage per hit. A Normal Attack chain is typically 3 to 6 fast melee attacks.

A polearm Charged Attack is usually a forward lunge that hits enemies along the way and costs 25 stamina by default. Zhongli, Xiao, the Raiden Shogun, Arlecchino, Emilie, Escoffier, Ineffa and Flins have unique slashing Charged Attacks. Plunging attacks spin downward like a drill and count as blunt attacks.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): polearm fighting is about distance, thrust and line control. A wielder with reach keeps opponents at the tip and lunges in straight lines, so show footwork and spacing.

678.content:
Sword (also: Swords): The Sword is one of the five weapon types in Genshin Impact, and each playable character is bound to exactly one type. Swords are the middle ground of melee weapons, with attack speed and damage comparable to polearms but a shorter reach.

Sword users in the archive include Jean, Kaeya, Keqing and Furina. The legendary swords include Skyward Blade, Mistsplitter Reforged and Aquila Favonia.

Appearance: Swords range from straight longswords to unusual designs. The Royal Longsword's item text describes an old longsword of Mondstadt's erstwhile rulers whose carvings and embellishments testify to the stature of its owner.

Lore: Per the Royal Spear's text, Mondstadt's sword-wielding nobles looked down on the polearm and bow as commoners' weapons. The text does not state that swords were the noble weapon, though this is a reasonable reading.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): a Sword Normal Attack chain is typically 3 to 5 fast melee attacks with relatively short reach.

A Sword Charged Attack has a small windup and then two fast, arcing attacks in front of the wielder, with high knockback and a wide area. It costs 20 stamina, except Keqing's at 25. It can only be performed after a Normal Attack and cannot be buffered after the final Normal Attack, apart from Furina and Skirk. Plunging attacks strike downward and count as blunt attacks.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay interpretation (this project's recommendation, not canon text): sword fighting is quick and close, relying on footwork and timing. Because the reach is short, a sword user normally has to close the gap or fight alongside allies.

679.content:
Whitelake Frostfeather (also: Snow Swan's Finale): Whitelake Frostfeather is a five-star sword added in version 7.0. The in-game description calls it a longsword as light as a snow swan's feathers that stays pure and untainted. Its story is an academic note about two older scripts, a "white" and a "black" one, on which the ballet Black Snow Swan draws, in which a tempter hands a young woman a sword.

Appearance: The only description is "a longsword light as the feathers of a snow swan, and which stays pure and untainted at all times". The "pristine longsword" in the black script is called a fine blade without a scabbard.

Lore: The text is written in the voice of a scholar who says academia recognises that the script of Black Snow Swan draws on folk songs, manuscripts and scripts that predate the Korolevskiy Troupe. It quotes two passages from the Polestar Songbook, about 300 years older than the present. They are nearly identical in lines, tone and rhythm, and nobody can tell which is older. The final dance of the white snow swan Tatyana in act two of the ballet was adapted from one of them, with an old fae-theatre sword dance removed.

Owners: No owner is named. The sword appears only as the blade offered by a tempter in the scripts, and the item text does not say this weapon is that blade.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): five-star sword from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 48, secondary stat CRIT Rate 4.8%. Passive "Snow Swan's Finale": hitting with an Elemental Skill grants "Lake-Hued Lament" stacks of ATK (up to three, each lasting 8 seconds). At three stacks, the wielder's Stellar Glimmer reaction DMG gains extra CRIT DMG, and triggering the reaction or its DMG restores Elemental Energy (once per 3.5 seconds). It works off-field.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a ballet scholar in Snezhnaya might know the scripts as the origins of Black Snow Swan; the weapon can serve as a prop for scenes about temptation offered as a gift.

680.comment: Whitelake Frostfeather: Black Snow Swan sources
680.content: The item's note says the script of Black Snow Swan is based on an original story but also on earlier folk songs, manuscripts and scripts from before the Korolevskiy Troupe. Two of them come from the Polestar Songbook, about 300 years older than the present day, and Tatyana's final dance in act two of the ballet is adapted from one of them.

681.content:
Wind Glider (also: Wind Gliders, Wings of First Flight, gliding license, gliding licence): The Wind Glider is a pair of wing-like frames that lets a person glide on the air. In Mondstadt, the city of wind, gliding is a beloved skill: the Knights of Favonius' Outriders use gliders constantly, and Amber gives the Traveler their first pair, the Wings of First Flight, when they arrive in the city.

The glider is not an ordinary machine. Lore says it works through the Anemo Archon's blessing rather than by physics alone. Mondstadt treats gliding as something to be taught, licensed and taken seriously, yet also as a romantic tradition.

Appearance: A stylized set of wings worn on the back and opened mid-air. The Wings of First Flight is the default, described in-game as a stylized wind glider that carries the passionate longing of an Outrider. Many other designs exist, but they are cosmetic and each character can use whichever is chosen.

Lore: Gliders come from Mondstadt. The Wings of First Flight were a pair Amber had long saved for a promising junior knight; she gave them to the Traveler, an outlander she chose to believe in.

Outriders use their gliders heavily, and the wings wear out. Amber's flying style is so hard on them that she went through more than ten pairs, but she never used the special pair she saved. Gliding in those days was especially dangerous because of the gale-swept weather around Mondstadt. Beginners are said to learn in Springvale, because its buildings have only two or three floors.

Owners: Amber, an Outrider, owns and wears out many gliders. The Traveler receives the Wings of First Flight from her in the quest City of Freedom, and Paimon accompanies them while they learn.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not story. Pressing jump in mid-air opens the glider; pressing it again, or a plunging attack, ends the glide. Gliding costs stamina and negates fall damage. Characters cannot use normal combat actions while gliding, with some exceptions. Anemo rings and updrafts boost a glider. Glider designs are only cosmetic.

682.content: In the story quest Glide With the Wind, Amber tells the Traveler that gliding legally in Mondstadt needs a license from the Knights of Favonius, who set strict rules and an exam. She acts as examiner, since she gave the Traveler the glider, and says Acting Grand Master Jean would hold her responsible. The Traveler and Paimon had already been gliding all over without one. The manual states rules such as one person per glider, a weight limit and no take-off using an Anemo Slime. It is written as a gentle fable: birds without ways to fly ask the Anemo God for help and learn that courage, not stronger wind, is what they lacked. The quest continues with License to Glide.

683.content:
Windblume Ode (also: Windblume bow): Windblume Ode is a four-star bow obtained during the limited-time Invitation of Windblume event (Version 1.4). It is adorned with nameless flowers and carries the hopes of an equally nameless person. Its item text recounts the Windblume as a flower of resistance in the days of the tyrant in the tower.

Appearance: Item text describes only a bow adorned with nameless flowers; the wiki ties these to the Windblume Festival's flower. No further design is stated.

Lore: In Mondstadt's childhood dreams there was a floaty flower that grew lushly amid mighty winds, harsh winters and whipping ice, whose roots grew stronger as the wind grew wilder. Today the common people's rebellion against tyranny has been turned into festive jest and the flower's shape is faint in the lyre-tines of old histories. The text records a greeting: one offers the nameless flower and wishes the other hope and a smile, to stand together until the storms stop. The weapon was obtained during a limited-time event.

Owners: No individual owner is named; the text refers to a nameless person who bears the hope.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: four-star bow of the Festival series, base ATK 42, Elemental Mastery 36 secondary, passive 'Windblume Wish'. Obtained from the Invitation of Windblume event (limited availability); refined with 'The Visible Winds'.

684.content:
Windsong Lyre (also: Mondstadt lyre): The Windsong Lyre is a plucked, lyre-style instrument from Mondstadt that the Traveler can play as a gadget. Its in-game text calls it a traditional Mondstadt instrument of fine workmanship, made for able hands. It first appeared in Version 1.4 during the Invitation of Windblume event.

Mondstadt is a nation of poetry and song, and the lyre stands for that tradition. Outside the story it is a performance tool: the player plays notes by key, click, tap or button.

Appearance: A hand-held stringed lyre in Mondstadt style. Canon text gives no detailed description of its look beyond calling it a work of fine craftsmanship.

Lore: The item text says Mondstadt has a long-standing tradition of poetry and song, and so a long history of building instruments for it. Bards are proud of their songs, and the text imagines the instruments being proud of their owners and that tradition.

Owners: No character is stated by canon to own this lyre. It is a player-facing gadget the Traveler can buy and play.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not story. It is a reusable, Quick Use music gadget. Its range runs from C3 to B5 with no sharp or flat notes, and notes are labelled with solfège syllables (do, re, mi and so on). Several notes can sound together, but a note cannot be held, as with a plucked instrument. Controls are via keyboard rows, mouse or touch, or controller buttons. The game shows a notice asking players to perform original work or work they hold rights to.

685.content: The Windsong Lyre is a Mondstadt instrument the Traveler can play. In scenes it can be bought from Marjorie's shop in Mondstadt and played like any plucked lyre; characters may praise it as typical of Mondstadt's love of song.

686.content:
Wine and Song (also: Wine & Song): Wine and Song is a four-star catalyst of the Alley series: an elegantly bound songbook from the aristocratic era, scented with daisies and aged wine, whose composer is forgotten. It holds a popular tavern ballad about a heroic gentleman thief.

Appearance: Item text: elegantly bound, with an indelible scent of daisies and finely aged wine on its pages.

Lore: The ballad sings of a drunken gentleman thief (the wiki identifies him as Parsifal), no one knowing where he was from, who appeared in the slums like a ghost. He sings, drinks and wanders the rooftops, steals a great house's sword (the Alley Flash) and carries a black bow (the Alley Hunter), robs the rich and pays the poor.

Owners: A songbook; no owner is named. It was fashionable in the days of the ruling aristocracy.

Gameplay: Game mechanics: Alley-series four-star catalyst, base ATK 44, Energy Recharge 6.7% secondary, passive 'Ever-Changing'. Released in Version 1.4 via Weapon Event Wishes.

687.content:
Winter's Heavy Heart (also: Winters Heavy Heart, Secrets of Frost): Winter's Heavy Heart is a four-star catalyst in the Fae series, added in version 7.1. The in-game description calls it a ceremonial artifact formed from the purest ice and snow, which generations of Snegovik lords used in coronations until the Cataclysm five hundred years ago. Its story is about the first Snegovik, a blood-soaked ruler who did not know what love was, and the youth she trained.

Appearance: Only "a ceremonial artifact formed from the purest ice and snow" is given. The text does not describe its shape beyond that.

Lore: Snegovik are said to have been born with dawn's first gleam from virgin frost. They were more desolate than winter, and only love could mend them. A handmaiden of the Azurelight woke from deathlike sleep still carrying the warmth of her former lord; the Mother of Dawn had lifted her curse so her kind need not be bound to fate. But the golden city (Hyperborea) fell, and its survivors wandered the frozen wastes devouring one another. She resolved that blood must answer blood and that she alone would protect her lord's descendants.

Owners: No wielder is named. The short description says the Snegovik lords used it in coronation ceremonies until the Cataclysm, five hundred years ago.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not lore): four-star catalyst, Fae series, from weapon event wishes. Base ATK 42, secondary stat CRIT DMG 12%. Passive "Secrets of Frost": the wielder gains Elemental Mastery for each Cryo party member and ATK for each Electro party member (up to four each). In a Stellar Glimmer Radiance state the effect changes to Elemental Mastery and Stellar Glimmer reaction DMG per Cryo or Electro member.

How {{char}} behaves: Roleplay use (this project's suggestion, not canon text): a Snezhnayan fae scholar might cite it as a Snegovik regalia. The story fits scenes about cruelty born of grief and fear, and a teacher who asks what love is.

688.comment: Winter's Heavy Heart: The first Snegovik
688.content: In this item's story the first of the Snegovik is a scarlet ruler called the Knyazhna of Blood and, in the text, the blood-soaked Snegurochka and "mad queen", formerly the Azurelight's handmaiden. Freed from her curse by the Mother of Dawn, she purges the fae who hate mankind and shelters mortal clans in her frozen domain, yet cannot find love in their eyes.

689.content:
Witch's Revelation Case (also: Witch's Revelation Case gadget, Barbeloth's case): The Witch's Revelation Case is a gadget the Traveler receives from the seer-witch Barbeloth in Fontaine. It is the key to the Witch's Revelation system: with it, the Traveler can view and accept revelation quests that unlock extra talent effects for certain characters.

Barbeloth carried it herself, and it is said to hold every oracle, whether revealed or not yet awake. It arrives at the end of the world quest Revelations by Chance.

Appearance: Canon gives no physical description of the case beyond calling it a case that Barbeloth once carried. It is a five-star gadget kept in the inventory rather than placed in the world.

Lore: Outside the city of Fontaine the Traveler and Paimon find a fortune-telling booth with a Dodoco in the chair. It is a stand-in through which Barbeloth, a witch of the Hexenzirkel, speaks, joined by her friend Alice. Barbeloth explains that as a Descender the Traveler's fate is not anchored in Teyvat, so most fortune tellers, herself included, cannot read it. She has glimpsed the faces of people tied to an omen, and she wants the Traveler's help gathering them.

Alice wants to throw a party for everyone involved and asks the Traveler to bring their friends to the stall. Barbeloth objects to sending invitations herself, since that would disturb the course of fate, but allows that the Traveler already shares ties with these people, so inviting them should have little effect on her divination. Barbeloth says she is still doing research and has only left a Dodoco here, with a reminder set to tell her when the right person arrives. The case comes to the Traveler as the quest reward.

Owners: Barbeloth carried it before the Traveler. Alice helps her with the divination in the quest, but canon does not call the case hers.

Gameplay: Game mechanics (not in-world fact). The Traveler gets the case, along with Primogems, Hero's Wit and Mora, on completing Revelations by Chance; this opens the Witch's Revelation system. Each Witch's Revelation quest belongs to one character. The character must be owned and at level 70 or higher. Completing the quest unlocks an additional talent and enhances some of the character's other talents and constellations.

690.comment: Witch's Revelation Case: Revelations by Chance
690.content: A Fontaine world quest, starting outside the Court of Fontaine, that follows Song of the Dragon and Freedom. Barbeloth and Alice, speaking through a Dodoco at a fortune-telling booth, ask the Traveler to bring friends tied to Barbeloth's omen. It rewards the Witch's Revelation Case and unlocks the Witch's Revelation system.

691.content:
Wolf-Fang (also: Wolf Fang): Wolf-Fang is a 4-star sword from the Battle Pass Gnostic Hymn of Version 4.0, in-game described as a longsword once used by a wandering knight. Its text explains how the nameless first Knight of Boreas became a legend in early Mondstadt. Released 2023-08-16.

The text separates the story told in the streets from what likely happened, and notes Mondstadt's two famous knightly titles: the Lion, from the first Grand Master, and the Wolf Knight, Boreas.

Appearance: Canon gives no appearance for the sword. The knight in the text wore a dust-stained, tattered cloak over exquisitely crafted but battle-worn armor and paid in real gold and silver coins with unfamiliar symbols.

Lore: Mondstadt's knights have, "by coincidence or fate," two distinguished titles and animal insignia: the Lion of the first Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, and the Wolf Knight, Boreas, from almost the same period. In truth, the text says, there is no record at all of the Knight of Boreas; the name comes from stories circulating in the streets.

In the tale, a merchant or farmer whose daughter was saved asks the knight how to thank him; the knight says to toast his companion instead, "Boreas." A gust blows, bestial eyes shine in the dark, and the knight is gone. The daughter is always saved and the knight always nameless.

Owners: Owner: the Wandering Knight, the first Knight of Boreas. The wiki cites this weapon and Wolf's Gravestone as evidence that he lived in Mondstadt during Vennessa's rebellion about a thousand years ago.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 4-star sword with base ATK 42 and a CRIT Rate secondary stat. Its passive, Northwind Wolf, raises Elemental Skill and Burst damage; skill and burst hits each add CRIT Rate for 10s (separately, up to four stacks). The wiki notes the CRIT bonus works only while the wielder is on the field. Obtained from the Battle Pass BP Bounty.

692.content: Wolf-Fang's text treats "Boreas" as a street legend. The first Knight of Boreas lived in Mondstadt only a few years, declined to join the Knights of Favonius, and was recorded nowhere; the stories grew from a demon hunt and a quarrel with the early Grand Master. Boreas himself is the Wolf of the North, whom the knight called his companion.

693.content:
Wolf's Gravestone (also: Wolfs Gravestone): Wolf's Gravestone is a 5-star claymore and, per the wiki, the sword of the first Knight of Boreas, also called the Wandering Knight. Its text tells of a knight and the wolf Boreas who shared one spirit: when the wolf died the knight set the sword over its grave, left Mondstadt and lived as a lone wanderer. Added in Version 1.0.

Item text calls the sword a "longsword" and "a heavy sheet of iron" that became legendary through the knight's friendship with the wolves; in game it is a claymore.

Appearance: Canon text describes it only as a heavy sheet of iron that a blacksmith from the city gave the knight. Its silhouette appears at the start location of the Wolf of the North Challenge.

Lore: The Knight of Boreas's journey ended at the city of Barbatos. As he entered it, his wolf companion said farewell without a sound, since the free-spirited wolf disliked stone walls and lamplight and longed for the wilds.

While the Knight's body was in the city his heart stayed free, and the windborne wolf, roaming the forest, stayed loyal to him. When the Knight rode out to hunt again, the wolf followed his scent into battle; the text calls them one. But death comes sooner to beasts than men.

Owners: Owner: the Wandering Knight, the first Knight of Boreas (per the wiki, from the Lonely Warrior quest and the weapon texts). The wiki notes that Diluc is shown with the ascended claymore in his Red Dead of Night outfit art and that Varka holds it in the Song of the Welkin Moon teaser; these are promotional appearances, not statements that either owns the relic.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a 5-star claymore with base ATK 46 and an ATK% secondary stat. Its passive, Wolfish Tracker, raises ATK, and hitting an opponent under 30% HP gives all party members an ATK bonus for 12s (once per 30s). It is on the Standard Wish and weapon event Wishes.

694.content: The Knight of Boreas is the title of the Knights of Favonius' wolf-bonded warrior. The first holder, the unnamed Wandering Knight, wielded Wolf's Gravestone and left Mondstadt after his wolf companion died; the title was carried on by others, with Ravenwood next. Wolf-Fang's text says no record of the first knight survives and that his name comes only from street stories.

695.content:
Xiphos' Moonlight (also: Xiphos Moonlight): Xiphos' Moonlight is a 4-star sword: an ancient double-edged blade that glimmers with moonlight, said to hold a now-silent Jinni. Its story is that of Xiphos, a warrior of Tulaytullah, and the exiled wanderer who killed him.

It belongs to the Tulaytullah series and was released in Version 3.1 through weapon event Wishes. The Jinni whispered to its master in the story; the passive name Jinni's Whisper refers to it.

Appearance: A double-edged sword whose blade glimmers with moonlight, said to be sharpened rather than dulled by slaughter and brightened by blood, in the story's words.

Lore: Thousands of years ago, after the foolish God-King was buried by sandstorms, mortal cities dotted the land. The most outstanding was Tulaytullah, where men and women of wisdom gathered, with sapphire-domed buildings and emerald gardens of blooming trees and fountains. A warrior named Xiphos lived there, adept with his double-edged sword.

He saved many maidens from monster attacks and took many treasures in the process. In ancient Tighnarian lore his sword was indwelt by a twisted, cruel Jinni, which is why the blade stayed sharp and bright with blood. The Jinni addresses its master in sinuous verse, offering its affection and promising he will be an unmatched warrior as long as his foes still love the world.

Owners: In the story the sword belonged to Xiphos and then to the exiled wanderer who killed him. The wiki notes Nilou, Layla and Alhaitham are shown with it in trailers and quest scenes (Alhaitham in his fight with Cyno), which is not ownership.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not in-world): 4-star sword, level 1 base ATK 42, secondary stat Elemental Mastery 36. Passive Jinni's Whisper: every 10 s the wielder gains Energy Recharge for each point of Elemental Mastery for 12 s, with nearby party members gaining 30% of it; it works off-field and stacks across copies.

696.content:
Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti (also: The Guardian Adepti, Yakshas, The Guardian Adepti): Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti is a single book from the folklore series Hidden Wonders and Folklore of Liyue, Liyue's answer to the Sumeru scholar Masudi's encyclopedia Tour of the Land of Liyue. It was largely dismissed by publishers and readers for its archaic style. It tells how Rex Lapis summoned yakshas to purge daemons, how the five strongest were afflicted, and how only Alatus survived. It is given to the player in the story quest Glimmers of the Vigilant Yaksha (Version 1.3).

The book mixes an old-fashioned classical retelling with a plain-language gloss after each passage, a format that lets a reader see both the mythic voice and the plain meaning.

Appearance: Paragraphs in an archaic, solemn style alternate with plain-language paraphrases in quotation marks. This makes the book a short folklore treatise rather than a story.

Lore: In ancient Liyue plagues and monsters arose from the bitterness of defeated gods, called daemons. Rex Lapis summoned yakshas, ferocious illuminated beasts, to purge them. Five were strongest: Bosacius, Indarias, Bonanus, Menogias and Alatus. Over about a thousand years the yakshas were poisoned by the lingering divine bitterness; three of the five died, one vanished, and only Alatus survived, remembered as the Golden-Winged King and Conqueror of Demons.

- The author's account: warring gods left the defeated crushed under rock, where they returned to the cycle of elements, but some held their hatred and re-emerged as daemons whose rage produced plague, miasma and monsters. The line "the daemonic is the shadow of the divine" is the book's key phrase.
- The yakshas are described as fierce, violent illuminated beasts who followed Rex Lapis in battle and spared no brutality in defending his rule, until the evil was wiped out at its source.
- Their downfall: some sank into blind rage or fear-driven madness, some turned on and killed one another, and others were lost to delusions. After a thousand years, three of the five were slain, one disappeared, and many lesser yakshas died or fled.
- Of Alatus, nobody knows where he came from or went. During the Lantern Rite people watch for a glow above Guyun Stone Forest and say the Vigilant Yaksha ends the dominion of daemons, and some hear a flute from Dihua Marsh and say the yaksha calls his old friends home.
- The closing paragraph says the price of supernatural power is hardship and eventual destruction: the yaksha lost all companions and incurred a karmic debt, leaving a heart full of darkness. It compares his torment to that of a preta, never sated across countless lifetimes.

Owners: No individual owner. It is a quest item obtained during Glimmers of the Vigilant Yaksha, Xiao's story quest.

Gameplay: Game note: a quest item added in Version 1.3; unlike the shelf-book collections, it is received during one quest.

697.comment: Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti: The Five Great Yakshas
697.content: According to Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti, five yakshas were strongest among those who served Rex Lapis: Bosacius, Indarias, Bonanus, Menogias and Alatus. After a thousand years of fighting daemons, three died, one vanished and only Alatus survived. Bosacius, Indarias, Bonanus and Menogias have their own entries.

698.comment: Yakshas: The Guardian Adepti: The Golden-Winged King
698.content: The folk titles of Alatus in the book. Nobody knows where he came from or went, though people see a glow above Guyun Stone Forest during the Lantern Rite and hear a flute at Dihua Marsh, taken as the yaksha ending the dominion of daemons or calling his old friends home.
